speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 106(8), I have the honour to table in both official languages the government response to five petitions.
[Editor's Note: See today's Votes and Proceedings.]
for leave to introduce Bill C-256, an act to provide for the conversion to civilian uses of technologies and skills used in the nuclear weapons industry.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the House that the hon. member shall have leave to introduce the bill?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to prepare for the termination of contracts for the production, repair, modification, storage or handling of materials used for nuclear weapons by encouraging the conversion of technologies and skills developed in or used in those nuclear weapons contracts to projects that serve the civilian sector and by preparing for the employment of individuals whose jobs may be lost by the termination of those nuclear weapons contracts.
I move that this be adopted.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
for
leave to introduce Bill C-257, an act respecting referen-dums and plebiscites in Canada on questions of public importance.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the House that the hon. member shall have leave to introduce the bill?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have in Canada an Elections Act which permits the holding of general elections as required. We do not have enabling legislation to permit the holding of referendums or plebiscites when required in the national interest. This legislation would be the enabling law for that purpose.
I think it is important to complete the panoply of democratic instruments at our disposal by having such a law enacted by this House, and that is why I introduce it at this time.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill C-258, an act respecting the establishment of the Centennial Flame Research Award to publicize the contributions to Canadian public life of persons with disabilities.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the House that the hon. member shall have leave to introduce the bill?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a Centennial Flame out in front of the Parliament Buildings and every year tourists who come here throw coins into it. I learned some months ago that all of that money is collected and simply goes into the Consolidated Revenue Fund. I felt

Routine Proceedings
that there might be something more appropriate and symbolic that could be done with it. The purpose of this bill is to establish a fellowship using the proceeds from that which are collected annually, a fellowship to be administered by the Speaker to provide research into the contributions made to the Parliament of Canada and the public life of Canada by persons with disabilities.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill C-259, an act to amend the Parliament of Canada Act (privileges and immunities).

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the House that the hon. member shall have leave to introduce the bill?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the members of this House have had undying privileges and immunities which we need to protect, but the public outside of this Chamber also has rights and privileges, civil rights and rights to privacy. This bill is designed to address those rights and to amend the immunities and privileges of the members of this House.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to present a petition on behalf of a number of citizens of Windsor, Ontario. This petition humbly prays and calls upon Parliament to reject the proposed goods and services tax.
In tabling this petition I want to note that several weeks ago the Liberals began a national campaign to enable Canadians to have their say directly as part of the parliamentary process through signing petitions.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I would like to call the attention of the House to the fact that the House Leader for the Liberal Party is going way beyond what our Standing Order say members are entitled to do in the presentation of a petition. I think it is obscene.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I think I had better deal with this right away. I regret the hon. member's comment. I do not think that is necessary.
There are a number of petitions coming in this morning and they will deal with matters of great importance to the country. There is, however, a rule that those introducing the petitions must do so in a brief manner and cannot stray beyond appropriate comments. I say, of course, with regret that the hon. member for Windsor West is perhaps going beyond that. I anticipated an interruption, and it has been made. I ask all hon. members to comply with the the practice in the House.
September 26, 1989

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect to the point of order, I had simply wanted to conclude and explain that the petitions we were tabling today were in response to requests by large numbers of Canadians to have their say directly as part of the parliamentary process by signing petitions.
We were beginning today to table petitions in conformity with the rules. We have very large numbers of petitions. We do not intend to try to table all of them today, but for days and days to come we will be giving Canadians a chance to plug directly into the parliamentary process to express their opposition to the government's goods and services tax.

maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the government through the party Whip has just shown its contempt for the views of ordinary Canadians.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I am afraid I am going to have to be strict here. I know the hon. member for Windsor West is rising on the same point of order as the hon. member from the government side rose on. I can allow some leeway, but I think this is getting into debate and I am going to move strictly to petitions.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I give you notice now that I respectfully ask you to request the Whip to withdraw the term "obscene", as I think it is a contempt of Parliament to say that a member in carrying out his parliamentary duty on behalf of Canadians when it comes to tabling petitions is doing something obscene. I think this is unparliamentary and it is an insult to the people of Canada, and I ask that you rule that the hon. member should withdraw his words.

maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would be very happy to withdraw any remark which the House Leader of the Official Opposition finds offensive. I do think that respect for Parliament requires all of us, and especially people charged with additional responsibility such as House Leaders, to respect the traditions of the House and the rules of the House, and I would hope that we will do so.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
This gentleman is the last person to give me, of all people, lectures on parliamentary traditions.
Routine Proceedings

maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: The hon. member for Calgary West has I think withdrawn the word which has been complained of, and again, I would ask that hon. members get on with presenting their petitions.

maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I present my petition I would like to rise on another point of order, and that is regarding the processes of having our petitions certified.
I think all members would have found that there is an incredible backlog at the moment in the office where the petitions have to be certified. I want to make the point that this is in no way a reflection on the people involved in the office that certifies our petitions, but many of us have had petitions in for at least three weeks and are still waiting for them to be processed.
Perhaps I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, and your office, to examine the problem and see if there is not some action that can be taken to rectify it.
We have an obligation to present the petitions that are signed by our constituents as soon as possible. To have them sitting in some office for three, four or five weeks is not acceptable.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I take seriously the intervention of the hon. member for Kamloops, and I know that other members have had the same problem.
I would advise the House that four more people have been assigned to deal with the petitions and, as the Hon. House Leader of the Official Opposition made clear in his earlier remarks this morning, there are going to be a lot of petitions. We will make every effort that we can to ensure that they are expedited as efficiently as possible.
The point is well taken, and I say to other hon. members, including the hon. member for Windsor West, that we will try to move these petitions as quickly as possible. It is not lack of concern for the importance of the subject matter or for the numbers; we are doing the best we can. If we are still having difficulty in a day or two, I would expect hon. members to make representation to me and I will see what we can do.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate your comments, and to assist the House, when the the government Whip rose to his feet I was simply trying to explain that we have a large number of petitions and why we have such a large number of petitions, but to assist the staff of the House we did not intend to try to table them all at one time.

Routine Proceedings
Rather, because of their volume, representing the feelings of so many Canadians, we were going to try to space them out over a period of time to assist the House and yet, at the same time, do our parliamentary duty. If the Whip for the government had simply allowed me to complete my remarks, we would have made a lot more progress than we have so far in the work of the House.

maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE

Several conditions apply to the presentation of petitions in the House during Routine Proceedings, the most notable of which is the prohibition on "debate on or in relation to" petitions presented in this way noted in Standing Order 36(7). Has the government taken any action to review the reverse-onus procedure found in Chapter 35, Part II, Section 8, sub-section 4 of the Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1987 and its impact on the nature of the transport industry in Canada and, if so, what action?
September 26, 1989

maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Procedures are now in place to evaluate the impact of the reverse onus provisions, among other things, of the Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1987 (MVTA). Specific provisions in Canada's new transportation legislation ensure that an assessment of the effectiveness of the legislation be made on a continuing basis. For example, the National Transportation Act requires that annual reviews be completed by May 31 of each year. In addition, a comprehensive review will be completed in 1992.
The National Transportation Agency (NTA) has recently completed the review for 1988, including the sections on new entrants, expansion and consolidation. These of course reflect the effect of reverse onus procedures.
Furthermore, additional monitoring procedures, under the auspices of the Canadian Council of Motor Transport Administrators (CCMTA) and performed by Transport Canada, the NTA, Consumer and Corporate Affairs and provincial agencies are being put in place.
These procedures will examine the effect of "reverse onus" on a province by province basis to determine if, by 1992, sunsetting of "reverse onus" is in the best interest of both shippers and carriers.
Sufficient time has not yet elapsed, nor sufficient data collected, to enable a substantial analysis of "reverse onus" to be accomplished. However, by 1990 some initial trends will have been established.

speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Forestry):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Forestry)
maintopic: PROPOSED ADDRESS BY KING OF JORDAN-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
The Forest Insect and Disease Survey, Forestry Canada, has reported damage to cedar trees in areas north and west of Ottawa and in particular from Ottawa-Hull to Brockville and vicinity.
The browning of cedar foliage is the result of two years of severe damage caused by an insect called the cedar leafminer, last year's drought, and winter drying or "winter kill".
Feeding by cedar leafminers has caused severe browning of the foliage and often subsequent twig, branch, or tree kill. Fortunately, however, severely injured trees will often produce new foliage later in the growing season. On individual ornamentals the infested twig tips can be pruned and destroyed in early spring.
"Winter kill" is characterized by tips of twigs or entire foliage turning yellow or brown in early spring.
Also, two years ago, there was a bumper crop of cedar cones which are retained by the trees and gives a brown appearance when viewed from a distance.
Cedar trees should recover if watered during dry weather. However, in natural forest conditions some mortality may occur.

The House resumed from Monday, September 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mulroney that Bill C-29, an Act to establish the Department of Forestry, to amend the Forestry Development and Research Act and to make related amendments to other Acts, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, I shall continue this morning with my speech on Bill C-29 creating a Department of Forestry, since I had to interrupt it yesterday because of time at five o'clock.
Among the initiatives which the partners can accomplish with the Department's leadership and participation is the development of the highest standards of intensive forest management for Canada's productive forest lands. Based on these standards, management plans can be developed which respect the important ecological role of forests, good conservation practices, and multiple use of the resource. The Department must take a leading part among the partners in developing a consensus about how sustainable development can be achieved in every region of Canada.
The Department can assist in developing a national inventory of the forest resource because we know accurate information is a key element of good management. We need this reliable database. It must contain site-specific information. To be meaningful, it will have to be developed according to agreed-upon standards. Without this kind of information, we cannot do the careful, rational and effective planning which will be necessary if we are to maintain our competitive edge. A federal department of forestry is essential in working with its provincial and private sector partners on this task, and in making such a database accessible to industry, government, and non-governmental public interest groups in every part of Canada.
We on the government side are well aware of the constitutional division of power and provincial prerogatives regarding forestry, and a new Department of Forestry in no way violates these principles. Our way of doing business is cooperation. We are already working with our partners within the framework of the National Forest Sector Strategy which finds implementation in Forest Resource Development Agreements between the federal and provincial governments.
In Quebec, those agreements were used in particular to finance site preparation, regeneration and tending activities over more than 650,000 hectares of land. At least 45,000 private woodlot owners have benefitted over the last four years and each year an average of 600 projects are carried out on Crown lands. We are now in a position to examine the last generation of agreements and to review what has been accomplished through this type of public management. Long-term goals and forest management standards are defined. More than $1.1 billion have been allocated for reforestation and forest management at the national level.

Government Orders
Federal resources committed for renewal and regeneration were strictly reserved to deal with the current backlog, not for lands currently being harvested which are 100 per cent the responsibility of the provinces and the industry.
The Minister has already announced that these accords, some of which are currently being renegotiated, will encourage the provinces to extend their planning timeframe toward more distant horizons as is befitting of a resource which takes eighty years of more to renew.
There is another task involving the provinces and private sector which the new Department can fulfill. It can develop manufacturing technology to add greater value and increase the variety of our forest exports.
The forest products industry must focus its attention on this task if it is to realize its potential for growth and expansion.
Canada's prospects in the paper and paperboard sector are strong. New technologies can keep our pulp production high. Solid wood products will remain a major component of the industry, expecially in panels and reconstituted boards. And the greatest opportunities open to us are in the value-added products.
We in Quebec, for example, have a major development opportunity in production of printing and writing papers, products which need inexpensive energy and abundant hardwood resources.
Since most of the products of Canadian forests are exported, it is a federal Department of Forestry which is needed to help industry and the provinces on a nationwide basis coordinate and accelerate efforts to keep Canada competitive in a rapidly-changing global marketplace which is constantly shifting beneath our feet. This means sharper marketing, focusing on specialty products, increasing product quality, shifting emphasis to a new mix of products. That brings me, Mr. Speaker, to the fourth mandate, the fourth task of the proposed Department of Forestry, namely to keep Canada on the cutting edge of research and development so that we can keep on top. The task is not ours alone. The private sector must also allocate more of their own resources for research. Our industry spends 60 cents on research for every $100 of wood we sell, while the Americans spend over four times that amount. One American company alone spends over 60-million U.S. dollars annually, which is comparable to Forestry Canada's entire research budget.
But it is not just increased spending: the research we do must become better focused, better coordinated, and become target-oriented. Our federal forestry labs and labs to which we contribute already are considered world leaders in certain critical areas that show best promise.
We can show, Mr. Speaker, by own example in research conducted or sponsored by a federal department of forestry that forestry research and development is regarded as a national priority.
By the way, Mr. Speaker, the Federal-Provincial Forest Resource Development Agreements have contributed to some 70 university research and other projects in the province of Quebec.
If we act and spend wisely, the dollar value of our forest exports could rise 55 per cent above current levels over the next twenty years, if, among other things, we emphasize new products and markets, and if we develop the technologies that will allow us to utilize our special Canadian advantages.
In addition to all these tasks, the new Department of Forestry will have special responsibilities in directing the management of federal forest lands, again setting an example with respect to sustainable development and multiple use of forests.
If we can show with federal lands that sustainable development pays off, that it is an investment in the future which pays handsome dividends, then perhaps we can influence those in the industry who act as if there is no tomorrow.
September 26, 1989

Last of all, Mr. Speaker, as its sixth task, a federal Forestry Department will be of great assistance to the other government departments having involvement with forests and forest issues. I can think of at least nine departments which are involved with significant aspects of forestry in their mandates, and it is vital that there be a lead Department to develop cooperative arrangements within the federal Government.
First, there is Environment Canada and Parks Canada, which have an interest in forest policy which might have an impact on wildlife or migratory birds or the effects of forests on the atmosphere and climate.
Second, agriculture and forestry have had a strong relationship in Canada over the last century.
Third, where it is requested to do so, the Department of Forestry could assist the First Nations of Canada with regard to forest management on their lands.
Fourth, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has other responsibilities as well which relate to forest management.
Fifth, there are Department of National Defence lands on which the Department of Forestry can demonstrate state-of-the-art forestry practices.
Sixth, a cooperative liaison with the Department of Industry, Science and Technology can keep forestry in the picture when it comes to research and development, industrial planning, regional development, and aboriginal economic development programs. And there is that all-important area of international trade, where access to export markets is of the highest importance to our economic well-being.
Seventh, Fisheries and Oceans understand very well the impact of forestry practices on the fisheries. Energy, Mines and Resources has an interest in biomass energy development. The Atlantic and Western development agencies are involved in ensuring that forestry reaches its full potential in economic development and employment in those parts of Canada.
In summary, then, Mr. Speaker, by introducing this Bill to establish a Department of Forestry, the federal Government is positioning itself to accelerate Canadian forestry's ability to fulfill its full potential in Canada's future.
Government Orders
Mr. Speaker, I have attempted to set out six of the major essential functions which the new Department could fulfill. This Bill is a further indication of the priority which forestry has for the Government. Indeed, over the last four years, this Government has increased the federal investment in forestry by 300 per cent.
As I mentioned when I began, Mr. Speaker, I wholeheartedly support this Bill, and I urge my colleagues to make this House unanimous in passing this Bill without delay.
Mr. Speaker, is there a question and answer period following this speaker now?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Yes, there is. The hon. member for Carleton-Gloucester.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Gaspe is to be commended for supporting the creation of a new department of forestry as proposed by the Government in Bill C-29. The Hon. Member spoke at length about reforestation, and I was glad to hear what he had to say on the subject, since our Canadian forests are the lungs of our environment. The Hon. Member had a lot to say about the United States and was lavish with his praise. He also praised what was being done in the province of Quebec. However, although I may have missed parts of his speech, I did not hear him refer to the other nine provinces. He seemed to be concentrating on the province of Quebec. I was also disappointed that he had nothing to say about the Gaspe area, his own riding where I am sure forests and a forestry industry exist.
My question to the Hon. Member is as follows: What kind of activities are we seeing in the other provinces at this time? Where is the Government going to make improvements, and above all, how does it intend to go about improving forestry activities in Canada if it is already faced with budget cutbacks and federal personnel cuts?

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for his kind words about my speech. Obviously, I spoke mainly about the province of Quebec, because I am better acquainted with the situation in that province. Of course the federal Government, through its new department, will be active in all other provinces as well. I may remind the Hon. Member that the riding of Gaspe is part of the province of Quebec, and so what I said about the province of Quebec, also applies to the riding of Gaspe.

September 26, 1989
Government Orders
I may remind him that in Quebec, 94 million hectares of land are covered with forest. That is probably why I concentrated on my own province. Its forestry industry includes 8 pulp plants, 49 paper mills, 121 sawmills, 4 plywood plants and 10 particle board plants. I think he will realize that the importance of this industry was one more reason for me to talk mainly about my own province.
In Quebec, forestry is responsible for 229,000 jobs, which means one out of thirteen. Sales of forestry products total 10.8 billion. Mr. Speaker, I think I had good reason to be somewhat partial to the province of Quebec, and I can assure the Hon. Member that when I say Quebec, I also include the riding of Gaspe.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the remarks of my hon. colleague from Gaspe. Given that the department of forestry received an 11.9 per cent cut in its 1989-90 budget, that 47 person-years were trimmed from the department, and that the new forestry department to be created by Bill C-29 does not have control over its own funds, in having to go a multitude of other departments and agencies, I would submit that the government is creating a department of forestry but not in the fullest sense. I humbly recognize this bill as being a modest beginning.
I would just like to ask the member for Gaspe, if he could possibly look ahead to the not too distant future, next year, whether the department of forestry would have greater autonomy by having its own budget. Would it be allowed to mature into a department that would have the fiscal resources it requires to protect and serve one of Canada's most precious natural resources?

Mr. Speaker, obviously, if we had been able to create a full department we would have done so.
The purpose of the Bill before the House today is to provide a framework. In fact, the department's authority will be quite considerable at the level of co-ordination. Later on, with the help of nationwide consultation, we will be able to give the Minister what the Hon. Member suggested and perhaps suggest a number of other aspects
the Government might consider, to give the department greater responsibility.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Forestry)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened attentively to my colleague from Gaspe (Mr. Marin) and I must say that his speech in general is very well thought.
One of our colleagues in the Opposition raised the subject of the Eastern Plan, saying that Dr. Marin, the Hon. Member for Gaspe, did not talk enough about it. Mr. Speaker, I know very well from a visit I made with the Forestry Minister this summer what people told us about the Eastern Plan; they were very glad to have the federal Government participate in a forestry program and they urged the federal Government to pass a bill to set up a full-fledged department as soon as possible.
Mr. Speaker, if it is possible, I would like to ask my colleague from Gaspe to describe the federal Government's involvement in quater detail and also to describe the reason those concerned want a full-fledged department, one that will really look after forests throughout the country, instead of going through a junior minister. So I would ask my colleague from Gaspe to give us some explanation of this.

Mr. Speaker, for someone, who did not want questions, I am doing very badly.
It is quite obvious that our experience over the past few years in eastern Quebec with the plan known as the Eastern Plan has been wonderful and this forestry program, we spent $40 million recently on private forests alone. On public forests, under the Canada-Quebec ERDA agreements, we spent a great deal of money-$150 million. Obviously, if every region could develop at this rate-the advantage is that all these funds, these programs must come under a federal department.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The period for questions and comments is over. Debate. The Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Belair).

Mr. Speaker, before starting my speech, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Restigouche (Mr. Arseneault) and congratulate him on the excellent speech he made .yesterday. It was very well researched and contained a lot of information that will certainly be useful in the years to come.
September 26, 1989

Bill C-29 will also have a major impact on my constituents. I would like to mention that my riding has four paper mills operating at top capacity and also a large number of sawmills which will be able to take advantage of what the new Bill has to offer.
Ever since Jacques Cartier set foot on Canadian soil, the lumber industry has played a very important part in our country's economy and still does. A century ago, there was practically nothing in the way of regulations that applied to the forestry industry. At the time, the Crown, through the provinces, gave individuals tracts of land which they worked very hard to clear, using the wood for the construction of buildings on their property.
Briefly, these people farmed the arable land they had cleared during the summer and worked as loggers during the winter, supplying saw mills and pulp and paper mills with the raw material they required.
At the time there was no advanced technology. In other words, tools and means of transportation were primitive, and that is why clearcutting forests was not as serious a matter as it is today. What I mean to say is that when forests were clearcut, the bare expanses were not as readily visible as they are today.
The forest was also a source of food, which shows how important it was at the time and still is today. Aboriginal people living on reserves depend on the forest, especially for their hunting grounds and trap lines.
The situation has changed today. The speed with which our forests are being cut has a dramatic effect on the Canadian Government's future vision and policy.

The forestry industry provides one in ten jobs in Canada directly or indirectly. In fact close to 800,000 people work in the industry, 350 communities depend on it, and huge chunks of income tax are paid to the federal government. Therefore it should only be fair that a lot of that money be put back into Canada's forestry to ensure its economic stability.
Yesterday the minister outlined the department's history which I do not intend to repeat today. Please allow me one comment.
Government Orders
It should be noted that since the turn of the century the department was bounced around on nine different occasions which explains its lack of continuity, competence and national involvement. There should be a strong federal presence to provide the much needed leadership. In this case it is better late than never for the federal government to impose its presence. Indeed, the creation of a department of forestry is a step in the right direction.
One cannot argue the generalities the bill offers, except in clause 6(c) where it only refers to the promotion of the forest industry but does not include enforcement.
I whole-heartedly encourage the minister to pursue the idea of hiring inspectors to oversee and supervise forest management. For example, he has mentioned that in Canada there is approximately one inspector for every
450,000	hectares of forested land, whereas in the United States there is one for every 15,000 hectares of forested land.
What I am saying is that it is not enough to advocate a forest management policy. It has to be enforced. The question is how.
The department does have the leverage power through the forest resource development agreements to impose its conditions on the provinces, namely in the area of reforestation and silviculture.

We have a lot of catching up to do. Canada's productive forests cover a total area of 220 million hectares.
Over the years, 12 per cent of those lands have not been satisfactorily restocked. We are looking at an increase of 200,000 hectares or nearly 1 per cent per year. Granted, 88 per cent has been reforested satisfactorily.
However, it means that next year, it will be 13 per cent and the year after, 14 per cent, and so forth. We cannot let a situation like this develop. We must act instead of constantly blaming the provinces. It is the only way to enforce the rules of sound forest management, as described in subsection 6(c).

September 26, 1989
Government Orders

Not enough emphasis can be put on silviculture and reforestation. Harvested land must be restocked. The notion that our forests are inexhaustible is totally false. This is where the concept of sustainable development is universally accepted. It is the means by which we can save our forests and prepare for tomorrow.
Subsection (d) of Clause 6 deals with sustainable development. In very simple terms it means ensuring that in 50 years to 100 years from now there will still be trees to harvest in Canada. We can no longer take for granted that our forests will exist forever.
As the minister is saying in The Green Ghetto, published in October of 1983, "The federal government must begin by putting its own house in order. Federal forest lands have the poorest inventories, the worst neglect of regeneration, and virtually no protection from fire and insects." Mr. Speaker, co-operation between the provinces, the federal government and the industry is a must.
I would go so far as to propose that the federal government enact strong legislation to lead the companies involved in clear cutting to reforest any area that has been harvested. If stiff penalties are the only way to get the message across, then let us not be afraid to impose them. Our future needs to be protected because jobs depend on it. The survival of those 350 communities previously mentioned should benefit from the vision that we, as legislators, have today. The minister's view in The Green Ghetto fully supports the statement, "Rapid action is needed just to protect the industries and their employees. Without significant improvement in our forest performance we will not only forfeit opportunities to expand, we will suffer rapid and painful deterioration".
Sustainable development should also be promoted because some regions depend on forestry as a means to develop and promote tourism. One example comes to mind. A few weeks ago I visited the town of Tofino, British Columbia, with my hon. colleague from Hamilton East. We were greatly impressed by the scenery. It is easily understandable why the local residents express such a strong desire to keep their surroundings intact. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, 57 per cent of the town's population depends on tourism. Can you imagine the devastating effects of clear cutting the steep hills that sculpt the background? Erosion of the top soil to the bedrock would undoubtedly prevent any regeneration. It spells
disaster. The spectacular sight it offers today would disappear forever.
I maintain that there is room for compromise, especially if forest companies across Canada would agree to selective harvesting, intensive reforestation and preservation of specific areas where nature would be forever stripped of its assets.
Another fascinating example would be the preservation of the Carmanah Valley with its prestigious spruce grove. These trees took 300 years to 400 years to grow; it would be a shame to destroy all of that within a few days.
Clause 7 of Bill C-29 stipulates that the minister should:
(a) promote co-operation,-with the governments of other
countries-
Co-operation, though, should not be a giveaway as it is the case with the softwood lumber issue. The government via the forestry minister has acknowledged that the 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber is terribly hurting the industry in Ontario and in Quebec. If I were an American, I would also be very reluctant to terminate the softwood lumber deal struck in December of 1986.
The forestry department should indeed stand up for the industry and demand that the deal be abolished. Failing the Americans doing so, the forestry department should request a hearing at the bilateral procurement board and take it from there. We should not go down without a fight when so many jobs are at stake.
Subclause 7(b) refers to the possible creation of a national data bank of forestry. According to the last Auditor General's report, "there is little information to assist Parliament in making judgment on the national Canadian forestry service program priorities as to how successful CFS has been in meeting its objective".
It is clear that with the rapidly growing importance of the industry such a bank is a must.

Bill C-29 does not mention unemployment in the forestry industry. Together with the Department of Employment and Immigration, the new department should set up a new training program for workers who have been laid off as a result of mechanization and advanced technology. It is alarming to note, Mr. Speaker, that in the forestry industry's logging and transportation sectors alone, unemployment increased in 1987, rising to 22 per cent. This is extremely high if we consider that at the time the national average was 8.9 per cent.
September 26, 1989

Government Orders

I could not conclude my remarks without referring to the desperate situation which is currently unfolding in the rain forests of the Amazon. Western leaders are creating a dependency by forcing Third World countries to blindly exploit their natural resources, namely forests.
It is hopeful that Canada will remain sovereign in its exploitation of its natural resources. A strong forestry department is the only insurance against the forceful hand of other industrialized countries.
The new department should have a clearly stated national responsibility for federal leadership in forestry matters, research and technology transfer, forest resource development agreements, forest resource data, industry marketing, trade and employment and public awareness.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member has another five minutes left so he does not need to rush through his speech.

I thought Your Honour was letting me know that my time was over.
To conclude, Bill C-29 has its weaknesses. I would like to think that the government in next year's budget will allocate the necessary funds to allow the department to completely fulfil its mandate and to exercise its responsibilities toward the most significant single industry in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend the member of Parliament for Cochrane-Superior on his speech in support of Bill C-29, that is, the establishment of a ministry of forestry. I thought his subjects of tourism, forest industry and especially employment and job training were tres a point.
He mentioned also about the depletion of trees. I wonder if he would elaborate on the importance of reforestation vis-a-vis the environment.

Indeed, it is a pleasure for me to answer that question. Reforestation, of course, is the major component of this new concept that has been thrown around for the last couple of years, namely sustainable development.
From the beginning of the century until the early 1960s, reforestation was not a major aspect of the forestry industry. For the last 20 years, companies and governments have started to realize that if there is not a very strictly adhered to program of reforestation, in 20 to 50 years from now there will not be trees to harvest in Canada.
Maybe I should be more specific. Now, most of the companies are within 50 to 100 miles from their plants. In 20 to 50 years they will be 200 miles from their plants. It is going to be extremely expensive for them to harvest and bring the product back to either the sawmill or the pulp and paper mill.
If we are going to endorse sustainable development, reforestation is a must. It is a major factor in ensuring the industry's future.

I would like to ask a question of the member for Cochrane-Superior. Actually, I would like to ask several, but I probably will not have time for that.
He was talking about that beautiful part of Canada, British Columbia. I do not happen to live in that actual area, but I have spent some time working there. There are beautiful stands of trees. Any one of us would stand in awe at what nature has wrought.
There are many, many groups of people advocating the preservation of such lands. But there are also many groups and many people whose jobs and livelihood is dependent on the forest industry. For example, the leadership and the membership of the IWA in British Columbia are very concerned that proposals to preserve these beautiful trees will also be taking their livelihood.
I wonder if the member would suggest how he would approach that situation.

I thank the hon. member for his question. Indeed , I addressed the same issue briefly in my speech.
What I saw in B.C., and I am going to use your words, was awesome. We have met with some environmentalist groups as well as with people from the industry. This is why I mentioned in my speech that there is still room for compromise.

Government Orders
I will come back to the same two examples I gave to you. In Tofino, the hills surrounding the town itself are absolutely beautiful. Right now there is a possibility that a company which has a tree farming licence may strip those hills completely, clear cut them of all wood. So, if you are on one side of the issue, can you imagine promoting the tourism industry and having those stripped hills to show to the people?
On the other hand, this is where the compromise could be. What if the companies strip only the side of the hill which is not visible to the tourists. That would be number one. In that manner it would not affect the tourism industry. There is also the possibility of selective harvesting. This would mean that one tree could be cut and one left to make sure that those steep hills do not erode. It is a very simple matter to say that if there is no topsoil on top of that bedrock it will not be able to grow another tree. If a hill is clear cut, then forget it, it is impossible to reforest that particular area.
At the same time, we could talk about sustainable development. The industry and the workers have to realize that today, yes, there are trees to harvest. But the way it is going now, in 20 or 50 years there will not be anymore trees to harvest and, therefore, some jobs will be lost. So now is the time to sit down and try to reach a compromise depending on each and every specific situation.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to make a few comments. I could not resist listening to the fine question from a member on the government side. That is one of the weaknesses of the bill. Bill C-29 does not address some of those issues. It provides for conflict all the way throughout.
There is a problem with a logging road in northern Ontario. There are problems in B.C. Environmentalists and industrialists are at odds with each other. What is the government doing about it? Nothing. It is just sitting back doing nothing about it. Bill C-29 should make the Forestry Department a little bit stronger.
My hon. colleague for Cochrane-Superior mentioned in his speech the replacement of jobs because mechanization and advanced technology is putting people out of work. What is the government doing about it? Bill C-29 does not address any of those issues.
Sustainable development is the key to the future. We hear the government preaching about the environment time and time again. What is it doing about it? It is mentioned briefly in passing in Bill C-29. The government talks about how important this bill is, how it was first on the order paper yesterday. It was promised in 1984 and there have been a lot of Order Papers since 1984. We have been waiting for this bill.
We support a strong Forestry Department. This is what the industry needs; this is what Canada needs, a strong Forestry Department.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. parliamentary secretary has a fast short question. I will entertain one more question and then it is tout fini.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with regard to the comments by the hon. member for Restigouche about northern Ontario and logging roads, I would just like to make it abundantly clear that it is a provincial matter, not a federal matter, and it has to be dealt with by the province of Ontario.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Forestry)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a comment for the Hon. Member for Restigouche. I believe that by tabling this Bill, the Government wants to strengthen the position of the department of forestry so that it can negotiate with other departments that are indirectly involved in forestry.
The Hon. Member for Gaspe pointed out earlier that there were at least nine departments that were either directly or indirectly involved in forestry. I am thinking, for instance, of the National Research Council which has a budget of $38 or $39 million for certain programs, money that is spent mainly on forestry research.
I would like to point out to the Hon. Member for Restigouche that since 1984, the federal Government has not acted unilaterally to force its vision on the provinces and on the industry. We have consulted with each province and all parties concerned. And this is exactly what the Bill tabled by the Minister of Forestry is intended to do: achieve a degree of co-operation, harmony and development that will be far more rational and more effective, instead of acting unilaterally as suggested by the Liberal Member for Restigouche.
September 26, 1989

Mr. Speaker, I have a brief comment. Under the Constitution Act, 1982, natural resources including forests are a provincial jurisdiction. From an environmental point of view, this does not mean in any way that the federal government should divest its responsibility for the forestry sector. The industry needs us and national parks need the federal government. We should take our responsibilities also.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak on bill C-29. It is a piece of legislation that has been an awfully long time coming. I can recall on August 30, 1984, during the election, the present Minister of Forests was quoted in the Prince George Citizen as saying that a full forest ministry would be be initiated with legislation immediately after the election. But this is only five years later, so it has been a while coming.
There are problems with the bill. I know it is going to be amended in committee. I am hopeful that the minister will see the light and see that there are areas of the bill that are very much in need of being properly beefed up because the bill shows little sign of a holistic, ecological approach to our forests. We have had for several centuries, in some areas of this country, all kinds of investment on the extraction side, on the manufacturing side, and on the technological side of the harvesting and manufacturing of products from our forests.
There has been little effort and certainly little money, either by the forest companies or by the provincial or federal governments, on the biological side. That is why we face the crisis that we do, which is something that has been identified by everyone from the Auditor General to the Science Council of Canada, to the Canadian Institute of Forests, and many other organizations from coast to coast.
I predict-it is awful to have to predict such things- but I predict that in 10 or 15 years from now in this Chamber, there will be another debate about whether or not to use the peace, order and good government constitutional powers of the Government of Canada, of Crown Canada, to invoke an entirely new approach to Canada's forests because of the crisis we have in our
Government Orders
atmosphere. I do not think the Government of Canada or governments around the world are yet taking seriously enough the problem with the whole carbon cycle and the dramatic impact that healthy growing forests have in reducing that crisis.
Let me take a quick look at the bill, before going on to one of my favourite documents entitled The Green Ghetto authored in 1983 by the present Minister of State for Forests, soon, I presume, to be the full Minister of Forests. What concerns me, is that the bill is awfully thin gruel, when one thinks of the size and value of this industry to this nation. One in 10 Canadians is directly or indirectly employed by it. It is our largest source of balance of trade.
The federal government, under Liberal governments and under Conservative governments, continues to return less than five cents out of every dollar taken from that sector. You cannot find another sector in the Canadian economy taxed in the way any of those areas are that get such a low rate of return from government, whether it be provincial governments or federal government.
One thing we have seen in recent months is the dramatic drive by the forest giants. There are only four major companies left in British Columbia. They pretty well control the whole of the forest land base in B.C. It is a similar situation right across the country. Certainly it is in New Brunswick where a very small number of companies control about half of the land in the province.
They have attempted to take hold of the words "sustainable development" and to change that in the public mind to mean "sustained development", sustained harvesting, without ever dealing and yielding to the biological reality of what sustainable yield really is in terms of the ecological wholeness of our forests, whether deciduous or coniferous forests anywhere in this country.
That section has to very clearly be expanded to send a signal, not just to provincial Crown authorities, but to the forest companies, both private and public sector, right across this country, as to what sustainable development really means. We know that even when one goes to the third page to clause 9 and finds what the minister has agreed to have in there through his legal draftspersons in relation to inventory.

September 26, 1989

There is not an accurate, adequate inventory, not only of our regional forests, but certainly not of our national forests. That has to be one of the fundamental roles taken on. I know the minister believes very strongly in proper, adequate, understandable, sound inventories. I would hope that he would be very co-operative in committee in seeing that that section is properly amended.
Let me deal for a moment with The Green Ghetto. I am sure you have read this document by my friend from Prince George-Peace River. It certainly makes good reading. This was written a couple of years ago but I will quote from the introduction which states:
Over the next two decades millions of people will work in forest related industries while millions more will use the forest for recreation and escape. But, on our present national course, by the end of those two decades, the jobs will be vanishing, leaving hundreds of communities with no other industry, and boaters and campers will find their activities confined to increasingly crowded "forest ghettos" called national or provincial parks. Disputes between industrial and environmental interests could become bitter. The social ramifications of reduced government services in provinces presently dependent upon forestry tax revenues will also be considerable.
Those are prophetic words, Mr. Speaker. That is exactly what has happened. In my home province of British Columbia, over the last five years, 25,000 jobs have been lost in the forest sector and we did not hear a peep out of Ottawa as to what could or should be done. We have had a $300 million jointly shared FRDA, made up of $150 million in federal funds and $150 million in provincial funds. The province wants to sign a five-year FRDA for $1 billion. But, as the minister knows, the actual amount put forward for forestry for the whole of Canada is down in the estimates. It is down, not up. I certainly have not heard the kind of remarks from the Minister of Forestry that one would expect from someone who published such a prophetic statement and has seen so little action in the last five years, entirely under a Conservative government, in terms of money going out there.
So what is going on is a bit of a shell game with the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Forestry saying, "Well, maybe we will sign a 10-year agreement. We will see if we can fool the public. We are only going to put up a little money so we have a $300-million FRDA over five years. Let us do one over 10, so at least we can have a $300-million FRDA over 10 years", or perhaps it is something a little bit more.
It is clear, contrary to what the Minister of Forestry has said in B.C. in my own riding, that there are not adequate numbers of trained technicians for intensive forestry, to get out there and to husband the forests. In fact, there are. People have been preparing themselves very well right across British Columbia and right across this country under the existing FRDAs to actually get into the big expenditure years which we have all expected. Certainly, I trust the minister will be signing a $1 billion FRDA prior to March, 1990 when our existing FRDA runs out.
Page 2 of this document known as The Green Ghetto states:
There are dozens of measurements of forestry activity by which our performance can be compared to other nations. One simple one is the number of foresters currently managing our forests. In 1982 Dr. Marcel Lortie, Professional Forester, estimated that only about 500 professional foresters were engaged in "on-site forest development. While our chief competitors (the United States, Sweden and Norway) have approximately one forester to every
15.000	hectares (34,000 acres) of land, Canada has one for every
450.000	hectares (1,111,000 acres). Moreover, as we improve, so do they. "If, in 10 or 20 years, Canada has attained the ratio of
15.000	hectares per forester-the ratio in these countries will have increased to around 10,000 hectares-per forester."-He noted that some countries practice even more intensive management - i.e. Czechoslovakia, with one forester to every 300 to 400 hectares (750-1,000 acres).
I have not seen much sign, Mr. Speaker, in relation to the expenditure plan we have, that there is any plan at the national level for a serious new body of professional foresters to conduct an inventory. You cannot run a popcorn stand unless you know how much popcorn you have. You cannot run a tire store. You could not be a farmer. But here is the federal government touting this new act, but without putting the financial muscle forward and saying: "Yes, we are going to take an inventory; we are going to do something serious about fires."
Almost as much land was burned so far this year as was harvested in this country. The military were never mobilized. Some comments were made by the Minister of Forestry years ago about the need for a broader base in terms of water bombers and the sharing of high-level aerial infra-red photography so that we can locate those fires before they start to spread. The technology is available now to isolate, through various forms of photography, areas that are having problems with disease or with insect infestations. We have to get much more serious about putting in the money that needs to be put into the largest industry in this country so that we can protect the forests that are there and manage them properly because they have been horribly mismanaged throughout all of Canada's short history.

At page 7 The Green Ghetto further states:
In 1983, the Science Council of Canada warned "The forests are essential to our social and economic well being; yet we have allowed them to degenerate to a dangerous point. We have been felling, selling and shipping timber for so long, and at such a rate, that today a 23-billion dollar industry is facing economic stagnation."
I am not going to quote too much of it, but at page 8 The Green Ghetto further states:
Almost 12 percent of our productive forest land is now in this dismal condition, and each year 300,000 hectares (half a million acres) are added to the backlog. If properly stocked this land alone could sustain Canada's harvest for about 30 years.
Again, let me deal with my own province about which I know the most in terms of forestry matters. The professional foresters in that province, through the ministry of forests, say that the sustainable yield in British Columbia is about 57 million cubic metres a year. The harvest this year, including private land that is being harvested, will come very close to 100 million cubic metres. COFI, the Council of Forest Industries in B.C., has predicted that we could harvest 166 million cubic metres.
As Dr. Bill Reese pointed out in B.C. this week, in a public meeting that I attended, the over-harvest that is going on in British Columbia is an over-harvest of almost 100 per cent. Professional foresters say 57 million cubic metres can be harvested and have sustained yield and we are cutting almost double that.
What does that mean, Mr. Speaker? We know about the fall-down effect. We know that our "nsr"-not satisfactorily restocked-lands are growing, not shrinking. We have the government playing coy, playing a shell game about how much money is going to go into the next phase of FRDA. We need to plan in British Columbia. We need to know what sites we are going to intensively manage; what areas we are going to get into seriously dealing with the existing soil erosion; what areas we are going to have to deal in a serious way with the kinds of undergrowth that have come up that are keeping the kinds of timber that are most suitable for those sites from growing back.
Government Orders
When I say holistic forestry, we are so far behind countries like Sweden that not only replant marketable, merchantable species of timber, they are also now planting seed grasses for songbirds; they are planting willow for moose. In Sweden, three times as many moose were harvested last year as were taken in the whole of Canada, and Sweden has less moose habitat than the province of British Columbia.
When we are talking about the forest we have to realize that we should not only harvest it and then just go in and plant a few coniferous or deciduous trees that are good for today, but we have to be forward looking now. The greenhouse effect has started. There has been a one degree Celsius change. We know how long it took the forests to move back up all of North America following the last ice age. It is a veiy slow rate of movement. We have to recognize that some of the sites that we are presently planting with certain kinds of species, will not likely even survive to maturity if the greenhouse condition continues at the rate that it is.
There is no sign that the Government of Canada, the Government of the United States, or the Government of the Soviet Union, the three largest producers of carbon into the atmosphere, are likely to dramatically reduce the amount of carbon going up in that cycle. That is why I make such a dire prediction that the next major debate on forestry in this chamber will be to use "pog" power: peace, order and good government, in relation to the severity of the crisis in our forests throughout the world.
On page 28 of The Green Ghetto, it states:
Not since Nero has there been so much fiddling, while so much
burned.
Well, nothing could be more true this year, Mr. Speaker. If you look at the amount of money spent and the number of people, and the amount of equipment mobilized to fight the forest fires that went on in this country, it is absolutely pathetic, if not criminal, that the governments in this country are so pathetically inclined to deal with fire and so pathetically inclined to deal with disease. It is something that this bill should be seriously addressing because it is in the nation's interest. If the provinces will not do it, I believe very strongly in a strong national government that takes these kinds of things on.

September 26, 1989

Here is what the minister had to say just five short years ago: "In addition to the water bombers, Canada needs high altitude aircraft with infra-red scanning equipment to detect fires as soon as they start". We still do not have one.
Yes, we do. Lots of them.

"Lots of them", says the minister. I would like to see the hours they flew while those fires were going on.
The Minister also stated: "Extraordinary work is being done in this area around the world today, but it is expensive and more shared cost programs will be needed if we are to have the technology available here in Canada."
Here is the ending. This is how the minister, while he was a private member, ended his report:
The paper was intended to show that our national policy has been to avoid decisions, allowing neglect to make the choices for us. Years of indifference have restricted the number of options now available and we are close to a time when it will not make any difference what we do.
Prophetic words, Mr. Speaker, because that is exactly what has happened over the last five years. Forestiy has been neglected at the federal level, at levels that will have incredible burdening consequences, not only upon our generation but upon generations yet to come. Let us look at why I say that.
Every year between 200,000 and 400,000 hectares are being added to what is called "nsr" land, not satisfactorily restocked land. One-eighth of Canada's productive forest land has deteriorated to the point where it can no longer regenerate productive forests. What happens is that the very thin topsoil, as other members have talked about, is often eroded following the kinds of forest practices we have allowed to go on to this point.
In 1983, 350 million seedlings were being planted annually in Canada. In Sweden, a country smaller than Alberta, 400 million seedlings are planted annually.
Sir John A. Macdonald, on June 22, 1871, 128 years to the day that this bill was introduced in June of this year, had this to say, and I quote:
The sight of immense masses of timber passing my window every morning constantly suggests to my mind the absolute necessity there is for looking into the future of this great trade. We are recklessly destroying the timber of Canada and there is scarcely the possibility of replacing it.
Again, prophetic words. Again, a Conservative, but in 128 years the Conservatives have not come forward with policies to deal seriously with forestry in this country.
We heard questions posed by a B.C. member and we hear them often from the minister. Why are we facing crises such as those in Temagami, Carmanah, the Stein, and the battle that went on over South Moresby? Only 2.6 per cent of this entire nation is adequately protected in conservation areas. The Prime Minister is quick to go to the United Nations and state that we adopt all of Prime Minister Brundtland's recommendations, and the World Commission Report, but that means we have to set aside 12 per cent of the lands in this nation for conservation purposes.
If you look at British Columbia that means we have to double the amount of land, parks, and ecological reserves in that province. We have to settle aboriginal title in the whole province of British Columbia. There needs to be a much broader, forward-looking, land use management strategy at the federal level to say what lands are going to be necessary to deal with the conservation strategy, to deal with the issue of aboriginal title, to deal with the crises we are facing in terms of marginalizing so much land that could and should be productive forest land.
Forestry can be and should be the bulwark of Canada's economy, but it soon will not be because of the irresponsibility and incompetence in both the private sector, and in what we obviously should have been doing in legislatures which simply has not taken place.
Even this year the Auditor General for Canada reported that "lack of adequate forest management has much depleted the forest resource. Significant shortages of wood are reported at the local level in every province. Restocking of productive forest lands has not kept pace with the harvest."
Those are the words of the Auditor General. So we have the Science Council of Canada, and the Auditor General, the minister in his former incarnation as a true believer in what could and should be done, but now he is having to deal with a cabinet who have recklessly kept him on the back burner. Why has he not been given a full ministry, and a deputy with long, sharp teeth, and a budget that can actually deal with these kinds of things? What kind of a reckless Prime Minister would keep a minister like that hidden away behind the curtain for so

long? Why has there not been debates in this chamber on forestry? Why are we not taking the kinds of proper approaches that we should be? Where is the billion-dol-lar FRDA that should be signed some time this month? Why is the minister playing the shell game about a 10, or a 20, or a 50, or a 300-year FRDA to try and cover the fact that his colleagues are being cheap and are chiselling the money away so that Michael Wilson can have $7 million to advertise the GST in The Globe and Mail?
Shame, shame!

We know his voice is not being heard yet, but from this side of the House we will speak up for the forests and encourage him to come forward with the kind of legislation that every professional forester in this country wants to see. They are waiting; they are listening. Those 400 single-industry towns are waiting to see whether the minister can deliver anything other than a small chicken egg. The seeds of revolution have been sown in this country in relation to our forests. We have to conserve. We have to properly treat our forests.
