Mr. Speaker, on September 6 this year, an article in the newspaper La Presse reported some comments I made about the PQ candidate in the riding of Chapleau which were also quoted by two of my colleagues yesterday here in the House.
These comments were labelled as being racist, and I am very sorry if anyone's feelings were hurt. That was certainly not my intention, and it was certainly not the purpose of the private conversation I had with the journalist in question, and I apologize, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, last July 30, Nova Scotia and Canada lost an outstanding citizen with the sudden death of Dr. Paul Anthony Johnstone.
Dr. Johnstone came to Canada from his native Jamaica 22 years ago. He became one of the pioneer leading figures in the fields of multiculturalism and human rights in this country. Indeed, his work at home and abroad contributed significantly to the position of leadership that is attributed to Canada internationally in the field of multicultural education.
At home in Atlantic Canada he was known as the father of multicultural education; indeed, as a prophet in our time. As executive director of Nova Scotia Human Rights Commission Tony Johnstone was one of Canada's very few, if not only, black deputy ministers. His contributions to intercultural and interracial understanding of our country was profound. He will be greatly missed by those of us who knew him, but all Canadians present and future are the beneficiaries of his work, his leadership and his contribution.

Mr. Speaker, this morning the finance committee heard from One Voice, the national non-profit organization for seniors. Since August, One Voice has been contacting every major Canadian seniors' organization to hear their reaction to the proposed goods and services tax. What it learned is that seniors organizations in Canada are opposed to the goods and services tax.
Why, Mr. Speaker? Quite simply seniors do not trust this government. They do not trust a government that promised to protect universality and yet has introduced a clawback on old age security pensions that will each year deny more and more seniors their rightful entitlement to universal social benefits. They do not trust a government that promised to make the tax system fairer yet has introduced a consumption tax that hits hardest at seniors on fixed income who will be forced to pay more and more of their income on basic necessities.

September 26, 1989
Seniors in Canada have learned that they can count on this government for only one thing, and that is the continued erosion of their income security.

Mr. Speaker, this summer's news that a team of scientists at the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto has found the fatal gene defect that causes cystic fibrosis is great news for all Canadians.
Led by Dr. Lap Chee Tsui, this medical team has made what someone called one of the most significant discoveries in the history of human genetics. Finding this gene holds out the prospect of an assault on cystic fibrosis from an understanding of its cause, the basic genetic defect, and its discovery will lead not only to diagnostic testing for carriers but also to the perfection of prenatal testing for the disease.
Our thanks to Dr. Tsui and his team for their dedication and hard work. Godspeed for their continued success.

Mr. Speaker, on June 5, 1989 we rose in this House to unanimously condemn the Chinese government for the use of brutal and excessive force against its own people in Tianamem Square. Within one month, the government approved approximately $230 million in loan money to the Government of China.
Since 1985 we have been hearing about the leadership role our country is taking with respect to economic sanctions on South Africa, and yet this year we see that our imports from that country have jumped up by an incredible 62 per cent.
These are only two in a series of inconsistencies that are giving our country a reputation not of credibility but of hypocrisy.
As Canada prepares to take up its seat as president of the United Nations Security Council, I urge the secretary of state to take this opportunity to prove that we are deserving of the position by reversing the trend and starting to honour our promises and to live up to our commitment.

Mr. Speaker, environmental concerns form without a doubt the most serious concerns of all parliamentarians in the world. Every nation on this planet is affected and could be permanently damaged if we do not deal with these problems soon. I have on one or two occasions voiced my opinion on what we should do to combat acid rain, so I am very happy to see other members finally coming on side. Canadians from across the country can be pleased at the recent emphasis everyone in the House is placing on the environment.
I rise today in order to praise a colleague from across the floor. The member from Broadview-Greenwood is to be commended for his efforts at the recent Conference on the Environment held in Toronto. All parties were present and even though all the problems of the world were not solved, we did take a few more steps in that direction. Every world class conference like this only helps us as Canadians show the world we are facing up to our responsibilities. This will only help in our negotiations in the future. To all those involved in the conference I say congratulations.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak about the now deceased spirit of free trade. Spirits are elusive and invisible. Canadians caught the spirit but the Americans have effectively killed that spirit.
I want to tell the House that the American steel industry is harassing the Canadian steel industry. Rulings two weeks ago imposed 100 per cent punitive duties against Sysco Steel and 39 per cent against Algoma Steel. If the ruling is upheld by the disputes mechanism panel, Canadian steel rails will be effectively excluded from the American market.
September 26, 1989

Everyone agrees the ruling against Algoma Steel was unwarranted, unjust, irrational, even stupid, but it is true. And what does the minister say? Absolutely nothing, not even a press release that his staff prepared. There is no guarantee that the ruling will be overturned, suggests the minister.
In conclusion, if the ruling is upheld we hope that the trade minister will join with Algoma Steel, probably all Canadian steel producers across this country, and with me and my colleagues, not only to bury the spirit of free trade but also the body of the free trade agreement.

Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative government has maintained a very strong commitment to the management of our west coast fisheries, a commitment that has been demonstrated very well this year by the record levels of Fraser River sockeye both caught by our fishermen and returning to the spawning grounds. The estimated horse-fly run of sockeye to the Fraser this year was over 18 million, the best since 1913. Over 11.7 million fish were caught and approximately 5 million fish were allowed to spawn to ensure that an excellent run will appear four years from now.
The Fraser River is a major beneficiary of the government's Salmonid Enhancement Program with over $42 million being spent on the west coast this year on salmon enhancement. Hundreds of British Columbians, including many school children, are involved with local salmon enhancement funded by the government. Successful management requires co-operation of the government, fishermen, industry, native groups and all British Columbians.
I congratulate the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and his staff for their outstanding work in the area of fisheries management and salmon enhancement and tell him that the fishermen who work the mighty Fraser River in my riding of Delta are looking forward to even better runs in the future.
5. O. 31 VIA RAIL

Mr. Speaker, as the associate critic for the disabled, I was outraged to discover that a disabled veteran was recently forced off a VIA Rail train beside a highway in the middle of nowhere after accidentally sleeping through his stop. The constituents of Hamilton Mountain and I-in fact all Canadians-are very concerned about this incident. That this shocking event took place at all shows how cut-backs to VIA Rail are affecting its employees.
I find it hard to believe that this incident would have occurred with a contented train crew. We all know that staff at VIA Rail has done its best to provide excellent service to Canadian travellers for year, so when a 76-year-old blind man is victimized I think we can presume that quality service including service for the disabled is now being derailed by anxieties over employment security at VIA Rail.
The disabled in this country are already being burdened by this government's cut-backs. Need they suffer more?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to highlight the impact of the free trade agreement on a very important area of the Canadian economy, that is, investment in Canada.
Canadians were told by the pessimists that free trade would cause investment to dry up and that our industries would close their doors and move to Alabama or Georgia to take advantage of inexpensive labour.
In the riding of Elk Island we can see that the opposite is happening. In Elk Island we see a $300 million new development in advanced industrial materials, a proposed $600 million expansion in the petrochemical industry, a new $60 million plant to produce environmentally friendly pulp industry chemicals, and a new pharmaceutical chemical operation. There is more, much more to come in the future. It is a future made brighter by free trade, a future that will mean more investment in Canada.

September 26, 1989

Mr. Speaker, when 174 East Indians landed at Nova Scotia two years ago, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Employment and Immigration launched an hysterical campaign, calling it an invasion threatening our sovereignty. Yet, when a rich businessman brags about buying a visa for $200,000, we don't hear a peep out of our brave Prime Minister or any of his ministers.
The Globe and Mail has again exposed a scandal of so-called investor visas for rich people who are not seriously interested in investing in Canada and may not even live here when they get their visas.
This Tory government issues thousands of these visas, over 3,000 in 1988 alone, while it deports seven times as many people to poor countries as to rich countries.
I call on the government to stop the investor and entrepreneur visa programs, investigate these rackets, close the loopholes and revoke the visas got under false pretensions. After all, if the minister deports penniless refugees when she does not believe their stories, why welcome rich cheaters? They are not the kind of people who build our country.

Mr. Speaker, the government's proposed goods and services tax is totally unacceptable to the people of the north, as my colleagues from this side of the House already know.
The people of the north already bear the burden of this country's highest cost of living. The food price index in Yellowknife is approximately 35 per cent higher than in Edmonton. Spence Bay has a food price index 96 per cent higher than Yellowknife. Living costs in the Keewa-tin range from 50 per cent to 70 per cent higher than the supply base of Winnipeg. Kitikmeot residents face costs that are 70 per cent to 139 per cent higher than Edmonton. The cost of transportation is the greatest factor in our higher cost of living. We simply cannot absorb an additional 9 per cent tax on necessities that are already many more times expensive than in southern Canadian cities.
This unfair tax will punish northerners in ways the government has obviously not thought about. I remind the government that a northern income cannot purchase what a southern income can. The government must reconsider. It must give special attention to the effects of this tax on northern Canadians. I invite the Minister of Finance to go to the north to see for himself.

Mr. Speaker, I have some sad news to report. The previously announced Liberal leadership stakes have run amok. They refuse to break from the starting gate. Race officials are now searching Canada's bushes looking for suitable entries.
The also-rans are just snorting that the $1.7 million entry fee will be for the rich and famous only. There is new speculation that the losers of the socialist turtle derby presently being run and difficult to follow will be invited to enter the gate of the Liberal leadership stakes. That disenchanted fans are calling for an inquiry and now the bookies are refusing all bets. Where is a dark horse when you need one?

Mr. Speaker, as the co-chair of the national Liberal task force on Canada's infrastructure I spent the last two months meeting with Canadian officials and environmental groups in several Canadian cities to find out the severity of problems with regard to deteriorating roads, bridges and sewers.
The actual statistics in all regions of the country indicate that the problems are far worse than ever could have been anticipated. With virtually no money to repair them, roads are deteriorating at an alarming rate. Raw sewage is being pumped into our rivers and oceans. Historically the federal government has always been involved, along with the provincial and municipal governments, in the cost of financing Canada's infrastructure. The federal government should share in the cost of construction and separation of sewers. Our beaches must once again be used for recreation and swimming, not for waste disposal.
Canadians realize that a healthy environment is the foundation of steady economic growth. When will this government commit to resuming its traditional role with
September 26, 1989

the provinces and municipalities in saving our cities and towns.

Mr. Speaker, in western Canada the RCMP uniform is a symbol of our heritage and must be preserved in respect for our forefathers and as a legacy for the future. It is imperative that we retain the distinct heritage and tradition of the RCMP by maintaining the uniformity of their dress code, with all the recognizable colour and trappings that have had such great historical value for this country.
I strongly urge the Solicitor General to undertake the necessary steps required to declare this uniform a national symbol of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. He will undoubtedly know that on CBC Newsworld last night the Minister of Finance laughed when asked about taxing food. He said the reason he refused to answer the question put to him yesterday in the House of Commons was because it was "a little parliamentary ploy by the opposition". He went on to say that to answer questions about a tax on food, and I use his words again, "just starts down that slippery slope".
We know that the Minister of Finance has already broken his word by putting a $2.5 billion tax on fast food and restaurants.
Broken my word?
Well, he intends to do this.
You better check that, John.

Yes, indeed. And he is unable to define, even after two years, what the definition of basic groceries is. We know that he is now
Oral Questions
playing a game in refusing to say to the House of Commons whether or not he is going to expand that tax on food.
I ask the Prime Minister if he will give a solemn, unequivocal undertaking to the House of Commons and through us to the people of Canada ruling out any tax on food.

Mr. Speaker, I suggest to the Leader of the Opposition that he check his words very carefully as to me breaking a promise. I said very clearly in December of 1987 that we would not tax basic groceries. He is now twisting what I said to his political benefit. He knows that that is true.
What we have put forward to the Canadian people is a proposal in the technical paper, which is a very well balanced and carefully structured proposal. This involves the goods and services tax, plus a number of fairness features, as part of that over-all tax system. Those fairness features include the exemption from taxation of basic groceries. It involves a very generous refundable tax credit. It involves a reduction in the middle income tax rate, a housing rebate and a payment to small business to offset the cost.
We in the government feel very strongly about that balanced package, but it is very important that we allow the finance committee to operate by not ruling out this or any other of the specific items which the Leader of the Opposition or the Leader of the New Democratic Party ask us about because as sure as we are standing here, it will be on food today, tomorrow it will be something else, then the next day it will be something else. Before we know it, the chairman of the finance committee will be saying: "What are we meeting for?" We say that there is a very important role for the finance committee.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, we are already asking that very question, but I believe that today we got the answer. Despite the fact that the Minister's intentions were kept under wraps, it would seem that he does want to put a tax on food.

September 26, 1989
Oral Questions
Mr. Speaker, on June 23, 1987, while making one of his more insulting comments, the Minister of Finance told the Hon. Member for Laurier-Sainte-Marie that there would be no tax on food, and he accused the Member of scaring senior citizens and the poor by talking about a tax on food.

Why is he playing cat and mouse with the tax on food? Why doesn't he act on the recommendations made this morning before the Finance Committee by senior citizens, and refrain from putting a tax on food? Why doesn't he say quite frankly: There will be no tax on food here in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, there is no game of hide and seek here. Our proposal is on the table and it is very clear. I think that the hon. member has pointed out precisely why we should not get into commenting on individual items that come before the finance committee.
Like food.

Yes, on food. He pointed out this morning, on food, that there was a group before the finance committee that said: "Don't tax basic groceries". Last week there were others who said: "Jhx basic groceries".
Who?
All of them. Last week they said: "All food".
Oh. oh!

speechtext: The hon. minister.

Mr. Speaker, the point that I want to make is that we will hear, in the course of the debate before the finance committee over the next few weeks, people commenting and making proposals on all sides of this.
It is not the responsibility of the government to comment day by day on these individual items. There will be a report by the finance committee and when that
report comes out the government will respond to it. Until then, we will not be responding to individual statements that are made before the committee.

Mr. Speaker, we are putting questions to the Minister of Finance on very important issues before the House of Commons. We receive answers that are either ambiguous or contradictory to those he has made earlier to the House.
Since he won't answer on food, I want to put a question to the Prime Minister on one of his priorities, on education.
The Prime Minister, through the Minister of Finance, plans to put the first ever federal sales tax on newspapers. He plans to put the first ever federal tax on books, including university students' text books. Further, most students will not be eligible for the low income sales tax credit since it is only available to people who make more than $6,100 per year.
Will the Prime Minister explain why, for the first time in Canadian history, there will be a tax on education, a tax on learning, a tax on literacy, a tax on instruction in this country? I thought that education and literacy were among his top priorities.
Mr. Speaker, let me clarify one thing that the Leader of the Opposition has just said. Students will be eligible for a $275 sales tax credit. That is very clear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: All students?

The Leader of the Opposition obviously has not read the document. It is $275.
The proposal that has been put before the House is a proposal with a very broad tax base. We have taken the decision as a government that we should not be in the position of making choices or influencing choices of individual consumers.
We have put forward that tax proposal with a very generous refundable sales tax credit so that low income people will not be disadvantaged by this. They will be protected by that credit.
We have also provided for exemptions for educational services, for libraries so that those entities will not be subject to additional tax as a result of the GST.
September 26, 1989

Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. The minister knows full well that his proposed action on VIA Rail flies not only in the face of reason but common sense and public opinion as well. It is patently obvious that the people of Canada want VIA Rail and they want it enhanced and improved.
Will the minister commit himself to give a reference to the Standing Committee on Transport and then use that committee report to modernize and enhance VIA Rail, to make it a modem transportation system, rather than trying to decimate it and wipe it off the face of the earth?

Mr. Speaker, I will obviously not make that commitment. We have considered many proposals. We have looked at many possibilities for VIA Rail and as soon as it is possible to make the announcement we will do it. But we will not return to the report of the committee.

Mr. Speaker, we have in Ottawa today over 50 mayors and municipal leaders from across Canada. They will be faced with the responsibility of providing alternative means of transportation when VIA is cut.
My question is to the Minister of Transport. It will cost $1.4 billion in severance and unemployment benefits to cut VIA, and it will cost $7 billion and even more to provide additional airport and highway facilities.
These figures are from the review on VIA Rail that the minister commissioned for $4 million. Will the minister refer to the business plan, the report on VIA Rail, and his recommendations to the transport committee for an interval and in-depth analysis before any move is made on VIA Rail?

Mr. Speaker, my colleague can think what he likes about the option we will choose for VIA Rail; it is not necessarily what we will do, but again, I do believe that we did consult. We recently met with the provincial ministers. We met with the Union of Municipalities. I met with the mayors of cities like Ottawa, Toronto, Montreal, etc. I think that we are now in the process of making a decision and, again, I do not intend to refer in any way to the Transport Commission or Committee.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. Yesterday when I attempted to get the minister to clarify the government's position on the taxing of food, simply to recommit the government to its own promise on the subject, the minister said I was playing a parliamentary trick. It is rather bizarre for a cabinet minister to say that someone who wanted the government to be honest about its policy was committing a parliamentary trick.
In light of what he has just said in the House, that he had no intention to respond to statements that were made in the committee or within recent memory in the House of Commons, would he respond to a commitment he made in the election last year on this subject, which was unequivocal, in a public debate and discussion on this matter on television. When one member from my party indicated opposition to a food tax, the Minister of Finance then responded on behalf of the government: "So have we, so have we", in response specifically to the commitment that there would be no tax on food without exception.
I want to ask the minister today: does he stand by that commitment that he made to the people of Canada in the election campaign last fall?
Mr. Speaker, we have made that commitment in the document itself that is presented to the House of Commons.

Then, is the House correct in understanding that if the government proceeds with this new sales tax there will be no new sales tax in any shape or form on food in Canada, as the minister said last fall publicly? Will he give us a clear answer to that? Yes or no? That is the issue.

Mr. Speaker, that is responded to in the document itself. Let me just make sure that what the leader has just said is taken accurately. We have made a distinction in the document between basic groceries and processed prepared foods. Those prepared foods, as we have said, will be taxable. They will not be tax free as will basic groceries.

September 26, 1989
Oral Questions
We will also have further discussions and consultations with the food industry to decide precisely how that is done, whether it is because of the establishment where they are purchased or whether it is because of the nature of the product itself. Those consultations still must take place.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister also indicated that with the sales tax credit system, this sales tax would not impact negatively on seniors and other people. But would the Minister confirm today that in spite of this credit, 570,000 seniors will be hit harder by this tax?

On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, I will not make that statement whatsoever because we have put into the sales tax system a number of very important elements that address themselves directly to the needs of senior citizens. The $275 per adult credit I think is available to some 80 per cent of senior citizens in full. In addition to that, the exemptions that have been put in the new system, including the exemption on medical devices, on basic groceries, on health care, on prescription drugs, on non-profit homemaker services, on meals on wheels, all those types of items, are specifically designed to address the needs of senior citizens. For that reason, I totally reject what the hon. member has just said.

Mr. Speaker, just a few weeks ago war was declared on workers and consumers in Canada when the minister announced his goods and services tax.
The Minister of Finance says that workers in this country must accept lower wage settlements regardless of what is happening with the cost of living increases that will occur as a result of the GST or Canadians will face higher interest rates, higher inflation, higher unemployment.
The minister says we have to have "wage and price moderation." My question to the Prime Minister is very simple. Will he explain to the workers of Canada what "wage and price moderation" means?

Mr. Speaker, I know that the Hon. Member will admit to the House today, as he has done on other occasions, that he believes that it is important for us to move from the existing federal sales tax to the multi-stage, value-added type of tax that we have, the goods and services tax. The key here is how we make that transition. We have set out very clearly in the technical paper how we believe that should be done to achieve the economic benefits that all the observers, all the economists say are there, provided we have a proper transition, a non-inflationaiy transition.
We believe that if business people and people in the labour sector will exercise moderation, then we will have that transition. We have said that if that is so, there will be a 2.25 per cent one time only increase in inflation, but because of the low-income tax credit and the middle-income tax reduction, the after tax impact of this is only 1 per cent. I do not believe that this is too much to ask of Canadians, both on the business side and on the labour side, to accommodate in terms of achieving those longterm benefits.

Mr. Speaker, in the technical papers the department keeps referring to wage and price moderation. The question is very simple. Does the Prime Minister and his Minister of Finance really believe that workers across this country are just going to lie down and accept this vicious attack on their standard of living?
We are asking the Prime Minister what his response is going to be when Canadians say: "This is not fair, we cannot survive, our families cannot survive". The government is not being moderate but it is asking Canadians to be moderate. I am asking the Prime Minister what his response is going to be when the workers across this country say no to the goods and services tax.

Mr. Speaker, I think one of the first places that we could start exercising moderation is with the language that we use in the House of Commons. The hon. member has referred to the goods and services tax as being a vicious attack. I have just set out the fact that the vicious attack that he talks about is an impact on people's income of 1 per cent. Surely that is not a vicious attack.
September 26, 1989

Let me go on to say that families earning less than $30,000 are going to be protected from the impact of inflation and that they will be better off after the change from the existing sales tax system to the new sales tax system. Surely that is a basis on which Canadians can show moderation.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance and I will try this time in French to obtain a clear, precise answer.
Can the Minister of Finance assure me that he intends to exclude food from the tax permanently or not?

Mr. Speaker, we have set out very clearly and very concisely what the proposal is for sales tax reform. It is set out in a technical paper. There is an overview paper that covers the broad parameters of what we are proposing to do. We have set that out as government policy.
If I am going to be asked to comment on every specific element of that particular paper and say if we are absolutely committed to this and this and this, then there will be no work whatsoever for the finance committee to do. The hon. member would be the first to be up on his feet saying: "Why are you pre-empting the work the finance committee is about to do on sales tax reform".

Mr. Speaker, I wish to put a supplementary question. I think that you can tell the Finance Committee right away not to waste its time considering a tax on food, and I think that all the members of the Committee would be prepared to admit that. So I ask the Minister of Finance once again: Stop evading the issue. Will you tax food or not? Are you changing your mind and going back on your election promises? That is the question!

Mr. Speaker, I do not know how many times I have to answer the same question. I have answered that question to him, to the Leader of the New Democratic Party and to his leader. Surely the answer is clear. It has not deviated from one to the other.
Oral Questions VIA RAIL

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. When the government found mayors and reeves across the country who supported the dismantling of Canada Post, it bought newspaper advertisements to herald the fact. I have in my hand a list of over 300 municipalities that have passed resolutions calling for full public hearings on any cuts to VIA Rail. Will the Minister of Transport listen to that request and ensure that there are full public hearings before any cuts are made?

Mr. Speaker, I have as much respect for municipalities as my colleague could have. That is the reason why I met with the Canadian Federation of Municipalities last June for more than one hour as I did also with the mayors of major cities in Canada. I will do what I have to do.
I believe, however, that the time is coming to make a decision and I will not postpone the decision about VIA Rail. As soon as the decision is made, it will be given and I will not change the timing of the decision.

Mr. Speaker, the minister has had on his desk a request from the mayor of Saint John, New Brunswick, and the mayor of Mississauga which I communicated to him on September 15, for a meeting with a delegation that is here in Ottawa today. This delegation is from Atlantic Canada and from the Windsor-Quebec corridor. They would like a bit of time to talk with the minister about why it is wrong for the government to dismantle VTA Rail. Will the minister either meet with them privately, today or tomorrow, or will he join others from the transport committee in the Railway Committee Room at 3.30 p.m. to hear their appeal?

Mr. Speaker, when I met with the Canadian Federation of Municipalities in June, the mayor of Saint John, New Brunswick, was there. When I met with the mayors of major cities, the mayor of Mississauga was there, I listened to them and I repeat: as soon as a decision on VIA Rail is made, there will be an announcement. Until then, I have no intention of holding further consultations.

Oral Questions

My question is for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. Under the minister's direction, Canada has followed sound conservation practices with respect to the harvesting of fisheries resources on Georges Bank. Unfortunately, the groundfish that inhabit the waters over the bank do not know that it is to their advantage to stay on the Canadian side of the line. Far too many are taken by the devil-may-care. irresponsible attitude of the Americans on the other side.
Given that it is unacceptable for Nova Scotian fishing boats to be tied up while Americans rape the fishery in Georges Bank, what actions are being taken to see that these resources are properly protected?
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe I heard the question.
The hon. member is right to be concerned about what is perhaps the most abundant groundfish resource in Canadian waters. It is divided by a boundary between Canada and the United States. The determination of The Hague line boundary some years ago brought great benefit to the Nova Scotia groundfish fishery in particular, and we insist that Canadian and American fishermen alike abide by our regulations and our enforcement measures.
It is a fact that the resource is much richer on our side of the line because we manage it well. We will continue to manage that resource well and we cannot tolerate over-fishing of the Georges Bank groundfish resource in any form it may take.
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the right hon. Prime Minister. On June 19 of this year in Halifax, Nova Scotia, the Prime Minister was his usual very eloquent self.
Hear, hear!

He said:"Either we ride the crest of the technology wave into the 21st century or we exhaust ourselves in the rip-tide of history".
In light of the government's complicity in the take-over of Connaught by the government of France, will the Prime Minister admit to us now that his Halifax words were as hollow as sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question of the merging of Connaught with another company is currently before Investment Canada. The hon. member knows that no decision has yet been made. Confidentiality provisions of the Investment Canada Act prohibit me or any minister from discussing that in this House, but I will tell the hon. member that the decision on that matter, as in all other matters, will be the same, that clear net benefit to Canada must be evident, and it will not be accepted unless it is evident.

Mr. Speaker, the government is missing the point. Even Investment Canada has said that Connaught is the strategic flagship for Canada's biotech industry.
What France needs surely Canada needs even more, and that is the point.

Even with the Government's promises regarding the sale of Connaught-and we know what to expect from this Government when it comes to promises-the question is quite straightforward: The French Government needs Connaught to secure France's technological future. Why are you helping them to achieve that goal?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question is wild and confused. We are not having a bid by the Government of France. We are having a bid by a company that is chartered in Europe that is going to merge with the Canadian company if it is approved by Investment Canada. That is what is before the House. For the hon. member to go from there into histrionics is really not called for at this time. Wait for the decision of Investment Canada.
However, I would advise the hon. member that Investment Canada not only will make sure there is clear, direct benefit for Canada on any decision of this sort, but in fact it will continue to encourage foreign investment
September 26, 1989

in Canada which has been running at about $3 billion a year from the United States, whereas Canadian investment in the United States has been running at $4 billion a year. Our investment around the world is strong. We believe in proper investment around the world including this, as long as there is net direct benefit to Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it has come to my attention that the 414 Electronic Warfare Squadron stationed at North Bay, Ontario, which, according to the Budget papers, was supposed to go to Ottawa will now remain in the best location for it, North Bay, Ontario. I am very happy that the people of North Bay will not have to go through the same ordeal that the people of Summerside are now going through. Now that the Minister of National Defence knows the cost of transferring the 413 Search and Rescue Squadron from Summerside to Greenwood, will he apply the same standard used at North Bay and leave the 413 squadron at its best and most economic location at CFB Summer-side?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the change in 414 was a change in the number of aircraft included in that squadron. That meant there was an additional cost for infrastructure which was not identified at the time of the Budget because of additional aircraft being placed in that squadron.
If we can get to the question to which I am sure the hon. member would appreciate an answer, the relocation of 413 to Greenwood will serve the maritime region, will continue to provide search and rescue services to the province of Prince Edward Island and will continue in the most cost-effective and operationally effective manner in the best area of Atlantic Canada, that of Greenwood, where it was located in 1968.

Mr. Speaker, I believe the Minister knows that 80 per cent of the rescue operations which have taken place over the past year have taken place in the general area of CFB Summerside in the gulf, while 20 per cent of the rescue operations took place in the new location which is Greenwood, Nova Scotia. I cannot understand how he can say that Greenwood, Nova
Oral Questions
Scotia, is a better operational base than CFB Summer-side.
Since the decision to close the base has not yet been reversed, I would like to direct my supplementaiy question to the Minister of Fisheries. In view of the fact that in six months' time, the tracker surveillance which does 600 of the 900 hours of surveillance presently being done in Atlantic Canada will be gone, would the Minister of Fisheries tell the fishermen of Atlantic Canada who will be doing the fishery surveillance in Atlantic Canada? What is the projected cost of this surveillance and where will the surveillance operation be based?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should remind my hon. friend and colleagues that the decision to end the tracker service was a decision taken by my colleague, the Minister of National Defence, because of the obsolescence of the aircraft. I can assure the hon. member that a full replacement surveillance capability will be installed before the trackers are removed, and I will have further details on that within the next few weeks.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The Minister has said repeatedly that no Canadian family with an income of less than $30,000 a year would be worse off because of his new tax. Our figures from Statistics Canada indicate clearly that
300,000	two-parent families with children are going to end up paying more in taxes than they will get back from the credit.
How can the minister justify picking the pockets of poor Canadians with this very unfair tax?

Mr. Speaker, there are a number of elements in that calculation. The hon. member has mentioned one. She has mentioned the goods and services tax credit. There is also the reduction in the middle-income tax rate. There is also the permanent increase in indexation related to the one-time only inflation impact that we expect from the tax. Those combined are what is behind the statement I made as to the impact on families earning less than $30,000.

Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, none of that has anything to do with the sales tax. The only way that the government can come up with these figures is by cooking its own books.
Would the minister confirm today that 300,000 Canadian families with children will be worse off when this tax is instituted? That is the bottom line.

No, Mr. Speaker, I will not say that. The hon. member referred to sales tax. The whole point I have been trying to make to this House is that it is not a sales tax, it is a sales tax system. It involves the goods and services tax, the goods and services tax credit, the reduction in the middle-income rate, the housing rebate, the payment that is made to small business to help offset the compliance costs plus the exemption on groceries. All of these are designed to provide very clear benefits that will improve the competitive position of the Canadian economy, that will allow us to get on with reducing the deficit, and also that will improve the fairness of the tax system, particularly to those low-income people to whom the hon. member has referred.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture. It concerns the crisis that faces the Canadian dairy industry today as a result of the yogurt and ice cream decision.
Last year the Minister of Agriculture promised dairy farmers across the country that they had nothing to fear from the free trade deal because he would be protecting the underpinning of marketing boards by transferring ice cream and yogurt and similar dairy products from the tariff list to the import control list.
We now know that this was not provided for in the free trade deal. The United States challenged it immediately and the challenge has been sustained.
I want to know why the government misled Canadian dairy farmers by saying that it would protect the marketing boards, when in fact it has not.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is inadvertently, I am sure, misleading the House when he makes that suggestion. This has nothing to do whatsoever with the free trade agreement. It has everything to do with GATT.
As a matter of fact, Article 11 was enshrined in the free trade agreement to ensure that supply-managed systems would be protected now and in the future. This is a GATT ruling. It was a very narrow ruling based upon an interpretation of like product. The panel determined that yogurt and ice cream were not like products and therefore did not impede the maintenance of the supply-management system for raw milk.
We have taken exception to that particular ruling. It has to be ratified by the total council. We have met with the industry and have worked out a strategy wherein we intend to pursue this with all the vigour that we can. The Minister of International Trade and the Minister of Agriculture are seized with this issue in consultation with the dairy industry. I think that the dairy industry is fully satisfied with the actions that we have taken to date.

This is not a GATT problem. It is a problem created by the free trade agreement. The minister knows that.
The Minister of Agriculture promised Canadian dairy farmers that the underpinning of supply management would be protected by the transfer to the import control list. It has not worked. The Americans have challenged this and that challenge has been sustained.
When will the minister and the government live up to their commitment to Canadian dairy farmers to protect their supply-management system? He knows that the entire supply-management system is in jeopardy because of this decision.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, of course we are concerned by the GATT panel decision, and it is a GATT panel decision, not a free trade decision. The hon. member should make it very clear. The hon. member is a fair-minded man. The underpinnings, as contained under Article 11 of the GATT are enshrined in the free trade agreement. Article 11 is in fact the underpinning of supply management and it is in place both in GATT and in the free trade agreement. We are going to defend it. We are going to defend it on behalf of the farmers of Canada, the dairy farmers, chicken farmers and all of those who are desirous of maintaining supply-management systems in this country.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the right hon. Prime Minister. Last week members of the Prime Minister's own caucus stated quite clearly that universality is a thing of the past. In September of 1989, the National Council on Welfare stated:
The clawback on child and elderly benefits is the most significant
change in federal social policy in a generation because it marks the
end of universality, a fundamental and long-standing principle of
Canada's system of social benefits.
I ask the Prime Minister to explain the fairness in dismantling the old age security system and the family allowance system, thereby ending universality and replacing it with a tax grab on young families and senior citizens of a 9 per cent GST.

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's premise in the question is simply untrue. The old age security system has not been dismantled in Canada, nor are we undermining the basic principles that underscore the family allowance or the old age security systems.
There is a fundamental principle here though and it is that the government believes that when Canadians are being asked to do something about the federal deficit, those of us who can afford to do so should be asked to cany the highest share of the burden. Those people who are most in need of assistance should be the ones who should be receiving the most.
The position taken by the opposition is that the wealthy should be immune from being asked to carry these burdens. What they are saying is that the top 4 per cent, in the case of senior citizens, should receive all of the benefits instead of being asked to cany some of the burden in trying to ensure that Canada's social programs can be maintained. We believe they are wrong.

Mr. Speaker, I remind the Minister that his own appointed National Council on Welfare said on page 7 that a social program that delivers benefits to everyone and then collects them back from some recipients is not universality.
Oral Questions
That is very clear from your own people you appointed to the welfare council. I say to the minister that you are discriminating against one-earner families-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member to put the questions through the Chair and to keep in mind the time.
My question to the minister is this: Why are you discriminating against one-earner families? You have a one-earner family-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry. The Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Fisheries. It concerns a recent free trade dispute panel hearing on a GATT decision that was opposed to Canadian fish landings in the province of British Columbia.
The minister promised the House that every effort would be made by the Government of Canada to protect the west coast fisheries against U.S. attempts to stop landings in Canada. The Inside U.S. Trade Today statement says that the Canadian Government has lost its first appeal to the free trade panel.
I want the minister to stand up and tell the fisheries people in British Columbia that no jobs will be lost and that the ministry is prepared to end the free trade agreement if this deals goes through.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is dreaming in Technicolor if he thinks he will get my positive response to that question.
In fact, we have put in place new landing regulations in order to enhance our ability to conserve and properly manage our west coast salmon stock. A free trade panel was established at the request of the United States to review these measures. That panel has not yet reported and, until they do, no further discussion or comment is appropriate by a member of this government.

September 26, 1989
The Late Dan McKenzie

Mr. Speaker, is the minister suggesting that Inside U.S. Trade Today and spokespersons out of the U.S. Department of Trade are incorrect in their interpretation that the panel has already met and the Canadian position has been totally rejected? Are you saying that you have not had a report to that effect in your office?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. minister heard the question and could respond.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International TVade):

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is my unhappy duty to advise the House that in view of the recent death of one of our very recent colleagues, there will be some appropriate statements given at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today as we all pay tribute to the memory of a man who has been a symbol of dedicated service and continuing commitment to the constituents of the federal riding of Winnipeg-Assiniboine.
The people of Winnipeg-Assiniboine will miss Dan McKenzie greatly. It didn't matter which party was popular at election time, Dan always came through with flying colours because of his proven record of speaking out for the grass roots right across Canada.
The loss is hardest however for his wife Marion and children, Karen and John. We offer them our most sincere condolences.
Dan will be remembered as a member of Parliament who anyone could call on any time they needed help in dealing with government matters. He would respond to their requests in a straightforward manner. There was no hedging or dodging the issues with Dan McKenzie.
He often endangered his own political future in the pursuit of satisfying his constituents. Dan never wavered when he spoke in the House of Commons. He never gave a thought to the political consequences that might result from his frank and honest statements on actions of government. He could always be counted on in the House of Commons to add to the debate and often bring
a message that reflected the views of ordinary blue collar Canadians in coffee shops, taxicabs and pubs.
Parliament was greatly enriched and as a result Canada served better because of the contributions Dan made in the House of Commons. Parliament needs more outspoken men and women prepared to stand up for the concerns of ordinary people.
In my relatively short time as a member of Parliament, my life has been enriched by the contributions of Dan McKenzie. I am proud to count Dan as a friend and colleague. I am sure Dan will always be remembered as one of the few outspoken members.
All of these qualities were clearly evident to the people of Winnipeg-Assiniboine when they elected him first in 1972 and sent him back to this House with enthusiasm at each subsequent election.
All members of Parliament express their condolences to his constituents who will miss the tradition he had established. More particularly, we offer our sympathy to his wife Marion and to John and Karen. May he rest in peace.

Mr. Speaker, I too rise today in the House of Commons to pay tribute to Mr. Dan McKenzie who passed away suddenly on August 15, 1989.
Dan was not only a colleague; he was also a friend. When I was first elected in 1979, Dan was already a veteran on the Hill having been elected as a member of Parliament first in 1972.
I remember fondly his willingness to help out us new kids on the block, as he used to call us, in any way he could. As the years went on and as Dan and I worked on a number of issues together, it became very obvious to me, and I am sure other members of this House, that Dan McKenzie was no ordinary member of Parliament.
He was a true spokesman for his constituents of Winnipeg-Assiniboine, often risking his own political future to ensure that the views of his riding were well represented in this House. To say that Dan was an outspoken Member of Parliament is indeed an understatement. But when he spoke out, it was on issues of importance to his constituents. At the same time Dan always held a great respect for this House, recognizing the honour and privilege it is to be able to stand here and serve this country.
September 26, 1989

A letter which appeared recently in a local newspaper really sums up what I feel best describes Dan McKenzie, and I quote:
-when all was said and done he was nothing short of a hero. If I could write his epitaph it would say, "he stood tall on principle when it was unfashionable to do so-Courage is easier to pronounce than it is to display-
To his wife Marion and two children, Karen and John, I would like to offer my sincere condolences and I would like to express on behalf of all colleagues of this House of Commons what I hope is their wish for happiness for the remaining family. Thank you very much.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to pay tribute on behalf of colleagues in the House and particularly the Manitoba Conservative caucus members, the caucus in which Dan served for many years and a caucus he chaired for some period of time.
Dan McKenzie was elected as the Member of Parliament for Winnipeg-Assiniboine in 1972, a year when a number of us from that province came to this House. Prior to that Dan had been an employee with Manitoba Telephone Systems. As well, he had been a member of the Winnipeg city council. Dan was elected in 1972 and held that seat continuously until 1988 when he chose not to offer his name for election.
As has been mentioned, Dan held many firm views. Those views were often in the issues which dominated the agenda of this House through those years. Those firm views were often very controversial, and I think for the record it is also important to note that he often was in a minority, both within our caucus and also within the House, on a number of those issues. But as has also been mentioned, he held those views not only firmly but consistently.
We can all take a look at our careers here and at that for which we will possibly be remembered. Dan will be remembered for two things, I believe; first of all, service to his constituents. I think he taught a lot of us the value of service to constituents, and he did that not only with pride but tenaciously. I recall as Minister of Health if there was an issue relating to pensions or family allowance, Dan would be at my doorstep immediately looking after the interests of his constituents. It was I think in that service in which his political success also lay.
The Late Dan McKenzie
Additionally, I think Dan will be remembered for his loyalty to Canada's armed services and particularly the membership he held in the Royal Canadian Legion. He spent many happy hours with his colleagues reminiscing not only of that war service but also the country as they saw it develop.
So may I, on behalf of all of us, extend our condolences to his widow Marion and to his children.

Mr. Speaker, I too rise as my party's regional whip for northern and western Canada, from where the deceased member, Mr. Dan McKenzie came, so that I may also convey my colleagues' and my family's profound sympathy and condolence to his family, to his wife, to his children and to his many friends for his service to the constituency and for his service to our country.
Death is the one chapter in the human journey that erases barriers and differences among people, even when we have differed. I am honoured to convey my colleagues' deepest sympathy to his family for the great loss.

Mr. Speaker, both as a Member of Parliament from Winnipeg and as a member of the New Democratic Party, I would like to join with my colleagues in remembering the life and work of Dan McKenzie.
Those of you who knew him, and you are many, will know that Dan was a very partisan guy, and I have no illusions that he belonged to my fan club or I to his. We often disagreed. I can imagine, if it is in the nature of things for people to know what is said after them, what Dan might be thinking about the fact that I am even on my feet.
I think, however, it is appropriate to remember the things that unite Members of Parliament in this institution, even though we disagree, and sometimes quite vociferously, with each other. I can remember many occasions on which I would receive mail from Winnipeg in which people would write: "You and Dan McKenzie are the only two sticking up for us," and these kinds of things. What did it refer to? Well, it referred to Dan's concern about veterans and pensioners. It is in that respect that I think so many Members of Parliament have come together and have worked together.

September 26, 1989
Government Orders
Despite all the differences, I think we are called upon to respect each other as members of Parliament and members of this institution and to take cognizance, as we are here today, when one of our colleagues has died.
On behalf of my colleagues, I extend our condolences to Dan's family and recognize the work which his constituents recognized time and time again in re-electing him.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock p.m., the hon. member for Skeena had completed his speech. The question and comment period following the hon. member's speech is now available to members, otherwise the Chair is prepared to recognize hon. members for debate. The hon. minister on questions and comment.

Mr. Speaker, I will not want to prolong the debate, having had a chance yesterday to say my piece, but I would be remiss if I did not thank the hon. member for Skeena for the incredible service that he has given to my work. As he and others know, us authors sometimes have difficulties getting our works recognized. The hon. member has quoted liberally and extensively from my publication entitled The Green Ghetto and I will send him another copy with my autograph. Incidentally, it is used widely throughout the country for fund-raising purposes. If the hon. member wants to use it for that purpose, he has my permission.
What I do not appreciate is having my record and that of my party mixed up with that of the previous Liberal administration. The hon. member was quite wrong when he said that nothing happened after The Green Ghetto was published and after the Progressive Conservative government came into being in 1984.
A lot happened, as he knows, in our province. The forestry resource development agreement was entered into which spent three times as much money as we ever spent before; $300 million. Quite an impressive record. One hundred and sixty-four million trees were planted in British Columbia; 137,000 hectares were planted;
871,000	hectares put in a management regime were surveyed. That is an incredible success story. We committed $31 million to a research facility in UBC, quite an impressive record.
Not only that, but the Prime Minister, immediately after the cabinet was appointed in 1984, appointed a minister of state for forestry who was immediately made responsible for filling the promise that was made previously, to organize and co-ordinate the activities of the federal government in forestry and to set in motion what we did in 1960 under the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker. You have a full federal department of forestry.
If the NDP had their way what they would be doing, I suppose, would be shutting down all the industry. There would not even be enough paper left to print their protest placards. They would have to carve it all in stone plates again. All I want to tell the hon. member is that it has been a long time since Moses, and a lot has happened.
I do want, in a positive way, to appreciate the positive attitude that he brought to the debate. I know I can rely on his support as we begin to go on to even bigger and better things.

The minister sounds like he is quite keen on Bill C-29. I guess he did not listen too carefully, but he is right on one point. I was interested in listening to the Liberals in the House today talking about where they really stand on this issue because during the 1984 federal election their current leader in fact came to Prince George, British Columbia, to a community dependent on forestry, and said that the Liberals were against, and I guess would continue to be against, a full department of forests. So I will have to listen with interest to how they try to set that part of that record straight.
September 26, 1989

Government Orders
As to the minister's remarks that an NDP government would shut the industry all down and so on, I know the minister knows better than that. That is basically what has happened to his shop, under the present Prime Minister. He has not been given the levels of funding that there should be at the federal level. As a matter of fact his budget has been cut by $28 million since last year. Of course there is no money there for the next phase of FRDA. As they say it is going to have to come from, western diversification.
As you will recall from this morning, Mr. Speaker, I pointed out rather well the shell game that the minister is trying to get into with his friend Dave Parker from B.C. although I think Dave Parker has the minister cornered now. The provinces are very clear. They are prepared to enter a $1 billion, that is a one thousand million dollar, five-year FRDA. The premier is on the record and the Minister of Forests is on the record. It would be irresponsible of the minister not to make sure that $500 million comes forward from the federal level so that we see that kind of a five-year FRDA go ahead.
I do not object to British Columbia putting more money in. The minister has quite correctly time and again in B.C. pointed out that with the replacement stumpage regime for the 15 per cent unnecessary countervail brought in by the Conservative government on behalf of the United States, many hundreds of millions have been collected. Stumpage in many areas such as the minister's own riding has gone from around $1 a cunit to anywhere from $7 to $20 a cunit that is being paid. So stumpage has gone up dramatically and Victoria has a great deal of money.
When the minister talks about the department and talks about where this bill is going to take us, I think we should keep in mind that there are not enough foresters and there is not enough technical equipment with the minister's department to complete an adequate inventory of what our forests really are.
The minister should keep a few things in mind. The same amount of forest in recent years has been lost to fire, insects and disease as has been harvested; something Canadians should be reminded of time again. Half of the harvested forest in Canada is not regenerating properly. There you have another half. We are already down to almost a quarter of the quality forest lands that we have.
The backlog of not satisfactorily restocked land is 25 million hectares. That is probably a very conservative estimate of what it is in this country now. Because of the GATT demand in every region of the country it will exceed supply by 1995, only five years from now. For every dollar generated by the forest industry in tax revenue, only five cents is returned. Of course, that is the combined return of the federal and provincial governments. That is not much of a return in terms of any other industry in the country.
Let us look at some of the other things the minister touched on in his question to me. In relation to inventories, the last inventory of Canada's forests was published in 1986 and prior to that in 1981. I hope the minister is not suggesting that we will not have another inventory nationally published until 1991.
Next year.

The minister is on the record now. He says it will be published next year, a complete inventory. That will be the tabling of the inventory.
I would point out to the minister that the problem with the current inventory information system being used by the federal and provincial governments is that some of the physical count information on which the inventory is based is 40 years old and the average on which the entire inventory is based is now almost 15 years old. We are dealing with terribly antiquated systems, terribly antiquated base information.
Even the latest information includes some startling facts. Fifty-five million hectares of forest land in Canada is not yet inventoried. We have never had a professional forester look at it. There is a total of 453 million hectares of forest land in the country. Over 500 million hectares of forest land in Canada was idle as recently as 1976 because it had just been burned over, and 200,000 hectares were gobbled up by pests.
We know that the Auditor General reminded the government what needed to be done but it looks like so far, and I would like to stress this point, the minister has been losing the battles in Cabinet. One thing I like to do from this side of the House is, through debate and through the minister, remind those reckless colleagues in cabinet, and in particular, the reckless Prime Minister.

Government Orders
I am sure if a reporter stopped the Prime Minister outside of the House today and asked him what is the largest industry in Canada, he would get it wrong. He would suspect that it was something other than forestry. He might think it was Gucci shoe sheds, or he might think it was agriculture-not a bad mistake to make but terribly erroneous.
He certainly has not recognized his responsibility fiscally in terms of the support he should be giving to the full ministry of forests in terms of budget, staff, technical equipment and funding for universities and inventories. It simply has not been done.
Let me give another example. I know you are interested in factual examples so that the people of Canada know just how badly this Conservative government is handling forest issues. Let me use my own province as an example. Between 1979 and 1987 the annual cut volumes increased in B.C. by 20 per cent while employment dropped by 25 per cent. The minister did not have much to say about that while he was speaking yesterday. Since 1950, in B.C. volume cut has increased 400 per cent and employment over all, over almost 40 years, by 22 per cent.
In 1950 B.C. had 2.64 jobs for every thousand cubic metres harvested. In 1986 the same thousand cubic metres produced only nine-tenths of one job. By contrast, California creates 5.2 jobs per thousand cubic metres harvested and Sweden generates 2.7 jobs per thousand cubic metres of wood harvested.
I am sure my friend from New Brunswick or my friend from Quebec, who sit on the forestry committee, would very much like to see this legislation amended so that we could get some kind of tie between areas that are harvested and the rate of reforestation, the kind of mixed ecological, biological reseeding and tending that should go on in those areas. We would like to see it tied to value added. I certainly trust that the government side will assist in properly amending this legislation which really needs to be amended.
