speechtext: There is no other member I would love to listen to more, if there was more time and we would be able to give him more time.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. Bud Bird (Fredericton-York Sunbury):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak this afternoon on Bill C-29, legislation to establish a new department of forestry in Canada.
I would like to just take a moment to make a point that the hon. member for Restigouche, the Liberal critic for forestry, commented on this morning when he criticized this bill as merely establishing the department of forestry. I would like to point out that this bill, which re-establishes the department of forestry in 1989, follows on the heels of the first department of forestry which was established by a conservative government back in 1960. A New Brunswicker by the name of the Hon. Hugh John Fleming was the first Minister of Forestry at that time.
I would like to make the point as well that in 1966 the department of forestry was diminished into a department of forestry and rural development and then in 1969 it was further diminished into the department of fisheries and forestry. Then in 1971 the Liberal government placed it under the jurisdiction of the department of the environment where it resided until 1984 when this government reappointed a minister of state for forestry and proceeded in the directions that we now are establishing with this bill.
I think that history reveals that it has been conservative governments, both the conservative government in 1960 and this conservative government in 1984 and 1989, that have acted to recognize, through a full department of forestry and a full minister of forestry, the very great importance of this resource and all it represents to Canada; a total of $40 billion in annual shipments,
800,000	jobs, capital expenditures of $6.4 billion, and all that flows from those facts and factors.
I would also like to take a moment to comment on some of the words of the hon. member for Skeena in his remarks. I think he also should be congratulated for recognizing the contribution of The Green Ghetto which our present Minister of Forestry authored several years ago and about which the hon. member for Skeena spoke with some disparaging inference. I would just like to say that for all of the wonderful factual words the member for Skeena delivers to this House, few, if any, have ever led to anything concrete, positive and creative, nothing to be compared at all to the creation of The Green Ghetto which has led the hon. Mr. Oberle through his years in this House to the point where he is now about to become the first full-fledged Minister of Forestry for Canada in almost three decades.
September 26, 1989	COMMONS DEBATES	3933
We have heard how vital the forestry sector is to Canada. I would like to speak about what a giant of an industry it is in Atlantic Canada. In New Brunswick the forest sector provides 38,000 jobs, that is one out of every seven jobs in the province. The forest industry has been an integral part of New Brunswick's way of life since the late 18th century. Today the economic importance of the forest is immense to our province.
The value of all forest products shipped within and outside New Brunswick total $1.9 billion per year, representing 40 per cent of all our manufacturing shipments and 47 per cent of the province's total exports. It accounts for 7.4 per cent of our gross domestic product. Close to half of New Brunswick's extensive forests belong to the provincial Crown and are harvested by leasing to forest companies.
Again, the hon. member for Skeena made a disparaging remark about the New Brunswick legislation and the New Brunswick approach to forestry. Again, he has missed the facts of the situation because in the management legislation pertaining to the Crown forests in New Brunswick, the New Brunswick Crown Lands and Forest Act, the structure, the system and the approach is established as the best example toward sustained forestry and sustainable development in all of Canada and has been acclaimed by experts throughout Canada and North America in those respects.
I would suggest to him that he go to New Brunswick and check his facts. He will find an approach to sustainable development that is well out in front of many of the experiences that obviously he has had. I would urge him to read the Dr. Baskerville paper on sustainable development in New Brunswick forests which I have sent to him and which he obviously has not read, or at least has not remembered. I think he will agree, when he has apprised himself of those facts in that paper and all the facts on the ground in New Brunswick, that the New Brunswick Crown Lands Act is a model of government legislation toward sustainable development in forestry in this country.
The federal government in recognition of the contribution which New Brunswick makes to forests and forestry has just recently completed the new federal co-operation agreement for forestry, an agreement that will commit $91 million between the federal and provin-
Govemment Orders
cial governments to forestry over the next five years in New Brunswick with a federal contribution of $50 million. That new agreement will have a special emphasis on the 36,000 private woodlots which are such an integral and important part of forestry in New Brunswick.
In that respect, Mr. Speaker, again in recognition of the deep commitment which our present Minister of Forestry has to forests throughout Canada, to the private woodlots of Canada, I would like to emphasize the action which he has taken this spring and summer in New Brunswick where, in anticipation of the delays and extensive changes required through the new co-operation agreement structure of federal-provincial financing which has been a fact of life in this year, 1989, he made a $2.5 million commitment to the private woodlot producers in New Brunswick. He assured them-literally putting his neck beyond the ground that most ministers would be prepared to cover-that he would provide to them the kind of ministerial assurance that would permit them to bank their activities for almost a whole year's work in reforestation and silviculture in anticipation of the agreement which now is about to be signed. For that I would like, on behalf of all New Brunswickers, to extend sincere appreciation to the minister for the commitment he has made and for the commitment he has delivered.
I would now like to go on to Nova Scotia where the forest sector is also an economic mainspring. In Nova Scotia, the value of all forest shipments approach $825 million per year. That constitutes 17 per cent of all manufacturing shipments in Nova Scotia, and represents 2.8 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product of that province. It constitutes 24 per cent of the total provincial exports, and a total number of 17,000 Nova Scotians are employed in the forest industry.
One of the big features of forestry in Nova Scotia is that it is in many respects a family affair with about 76 per cent of the forests in Nova Scotia being privately owned. One of those energetic parts of the entire forest industry in Nova Scotia is the Christmas tree industry. Nova Scotia's Christmas tree industry mainly uses balsam fir. About a third is cut by big operators with 500 to 2,500 acres in holdings, another third by medium-sized operators with lots averaging 100 to 400 acres and the remainder from small woodlots of less than 100 acres.

September 26, 1989
Government Orders
The people of the industry have that old Nova Scotia virtue of self-reliance. The industry benefits from research and technical assistance on disease and insect control. But the men and women in the industry in Nova Scotia are not looking for grants or hand-outs. In fact, they have conscientiously and publicly refused anything that smacks of a subsidy.
There are about 2,500 Christmas tree growers in Nova Scotia, Mr. Speaker, and most are woodlot operators who do other kinds of growing. About 95 per cent of the crop is exported to the United States, representing a $30 million economic activity annually, providing 500 fulltime jobs and up to 3,000 part-time jobs.
Every year these Nova Scotians cut and ship 1,750,000 Christmas trees. They make and ship upwards to 300,000 wreaths, and about 50,000, 25 pound bails of brush. The Christmas tree business and the Christmas tree forest industry is a big thing to Nova Scotia. The federal government has recognized the value of forestry in Nova Scotia. Over the past five years it has contributed a total of $57.7 million toward forest management and renewal with a new agreement now in the latter stages of negotiation.
In Prince Edward Island, Canada's smallest province, a lot of woodland during the 1920s and 1930s was cleared for farming. The stands that were left were allowed to decline and have become overgrown with white spruce, poplar and white birch. These are species with limited commercial value. They are now overly mature and susceptible to disease and insects.
These stands are now being replaced by stands of more commercially useful species such as black spruce, white pine and eastern larch. The plan is to manage these new stands on a sustainable basis.
What is happening to the old stands that have been cleared away? That wood is being used in an interesting biomass conversion project. It is, in fact, chipped and fuels Charlottetown's district heating system which heats much of the city's downtown core. This was the first such system in the entire country and is an example of the creativity of islanders.
The forestry sector is important to the island. It employs 2 per cent of the labour force and generates $1.4 million in exports.
In Newfoundland, the forest industry provides 10,000 jobs. It represents 6 per cent of the total labour force. One in eighteen workers depend on forestry. Exports alone come to $372 million, or 25 per cent of all exports from the province.
Again, federal-provincial co-operation have been the watchwords. Since fiscal year 1986-87, the federal government has contributed $24.6 million toward forest management and renewal under the Canada-Newfound-land Forest Resource Development Agreement.
This year, the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency signed a $53 million agreement with Newfoundland to benefit Labrador; $6 million of which involves the development of the forest industry in the Goose Bay region around the upper and lower Churchill Falls.
Forestry Canada is co-operating in that initiative. It is working with the provincial Forestry Department in Newfoundland to accomplish some specific things: first, to carry out a forest inventory of the region; second, to establish a forest management program for the region; and, lastly, to perform an environmental sensitivity analysis which will allow us to cut in a way that is reconcilable with the principles of sustainable development.
This region of Labrador, where there is almost no cutting now, is a region that will help Canada meet the anticipated jump in world demand for our forest products. The program in Labrador is an example of federal-provincial co-operation.

But Mr. Speaker, there is a lot more. This is just a sample of what sustainable development will be like. We can see how Canadians are facing up to the trade challenges of the next century as they prepare to increase their productivity while preserving the environment.
There is an important message in that program. Before making major cuts, we must analyse any relevant data to minimize the impact of operations on the environment and to ensure optimum economic spin-offs for the regions.
September 26, 1989

That approach will meet the future needs of Canadians. Through federal-provincial co-operation, we will decide on the best course to follow before taking action.

I have tried to show how important the forest sector is to Atlantic Canada. What we do in Atlantic Canada is a mirror, a model for the rest of the country. In a region where most economic activity flows from nature's gifts, every initiative that protects nature will be enthusiastically embraced.
Others have talked about the need to ensure environmentally sustainable economic development. There is not an Atlantic Canadian for whom that notion does not have special meaning. How can we extend that model and pursue that concept in a national manner across Canada? How can we bring ten provinces and two territories and the federal government to some semblance of a common approach? How can we motivate industry to participate in a consistent manner with all jurisdictions? How can we exert a parallel influence on private industrial land and smaller woodlots? How can we establish sustained development in all of Canada's forests?
The federal government recognizes that most forests are provincial responsibilities. It realizes that each jurisdiction will probably have its own unique options to consider. But there can be an integrated approach and a common commitment to the principles of sustainable development in our forests.
For example, the Council of Provincial Resource Ministers is certainly one avenue for this approach. In particular, I believe the new federal department of forestry should have a binding role to play, to be the glue in the process, much in the same manner as it has consistently provided research and development assistance to the provinces in such areas as forest biology, fire control, and insecticide and herbicides treatment. The Canadian Forest Service can build on the New Brunswick model and the Labrador model to help the rest of the country in specific ways; first, by co-ordinating technological practices with regard to such things as forest inventories and geographic information systems. It is a fact that consistent forest data is difficult to obtain for all 10 provinces in any integrated manner.
Government Orders
The federal department of forestry can help to develop common methods for analyzing management problems. The federal department of forestry can write model specifications on both environmental and developmental goals for adoption by each province within their respective jurisdictions leading to sustainable development.
The Government of Canada could help set an example with more sustained development of its own lands. This might necessarily require extensive consolidation for forest management responsibilities among such departments as Forestry, Environment, Indian Affairs, Energy, Mines and Resources, and the Department of National Defence.
As well, industrial development and international marketing functions for forest products might well be integrated eventually within the new department of forestry so that the concepts of finished product and added value would be in context and harmony with the state and the management of the resource itself.
Sustained development demands that we marry the end uses to the available resources. Such a transfer of these responsibilities from the present Department of Industry, Science and Technology would provide the forestry minister with a vital and consistent linkage to the forest industry and would extend his opportunities for influencing industrial participation in the process of sustained management of our forests right across Canada.
The present administration of federal-provincial forestry agreements should be intensified under the forestry minister, preferably on longer-term schedules to match the nature of the forest resource than is the case for the present five-year cycles. His influence in terms of a national program for sustained development can be made to reach Canada's private woodlot owners who are among the primary beneficiaries of the funding agreement.
In these and other ways, Mr. Speaker, the federal minister of forestry can play an important guiding role for sustained development in Canada's forests. It seems a special opportunity that, at almost the same moment in history when the concepts of sustained development have come to the fore of public consciousness about our forests, the federal government has given rebirth to a national department of forestry.

September 26, 1989
Government Orders
Our job now is to pass this legislation to create this department of forestry, and then to embark upon the road that the standing committee on forestry has already anticipated when, on May 31, we reached agreement in principle for an approach to a list of the kinds of examinations to help to develop on a national basis in Canada, hopefully to assist the minister of forestry and the staff of the department of forestry, in building, flowering and flourishing their future role on behalf of this most important of Canada's resources.
I would like to read two or three of the subject areas that we propose to address to the new department of forestry in terms of promoting public awareness of and support for the significance of Canada's forest resources in all aspects: economical, environmental, ecological and recreational. They are co-operating with provinces and industry to develop the highest standards of intensive forest management on a multiple use and sustainable development basis for all forest lands in Canada; co-operating with the provinces and industry to develop the highest potential of manufacturing technology and add-ed-value utilization for Canada's forest resources; maintaining and expanding the research and development activities of the Canadian Forestry Service, by directing intensive management of federal forest lands on a multiple-use sustainable-development basis; and co-ordination and co-operation with all of the other government departments-Environment, Parks Canada for wildlife, migratory birds, pesticides, herbicides, and so on.
They also include co-ordinating with Agriculture with respect to herbicides and pesticides, with Indian and Northern Affairs, with Fisheries and Oceans, with National Defence, with International Trade, with Industry, Science and Technology, with Energy, Mines and Resources, with the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and the Western Diversification Fund. In all of these manners the new department of forestry can help to lead the way for the enhancement and the sustainabililty for for the long, long-term future of Canada's forests.
We should now be ready in all areas of Canada to do something about sustainable development in our forests. With Bill C-29, when we get it passed and passed quickly, when we get this new department alive and in action, we will take a big step forward. Now let us get on with the job.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the member from Fredericton on his speech. There are a number of issues that the member forgot to address-I do not know if it was intentional or not-namely, the decrease of 11.9 per cent budget dollars for this year's forestry department.
Would the member not agree that if we are going to have a strong forestry department in Canada that at least we should have the budget to support it?

Mr. Speaker, I think that in due course we will have the budget to support it. I have some figures here that I would like to use to respond to the very legitimate question.
As I said in my remarks, we, on the Standing Committee on Forestry and Fisheries of which the hon. member is a member, discussed the fact that this legislation was the beginning. It was to give rebirth to the structure of the department of forestry. It is really a very short piece of legislation and does not have the encompassing purposes which we will some day see the department of forestry co-ordinating in the near term and perhaps in due course fully conducting on behalf of the Government of Canada.
The Main Estimates, however, for 1989-90 do not take into account the resources which have been negotiated as part of the process in establishing the new department of forestry. In addition to those figures I am told that 35 person years and $1.7 million have been transferred from Agriculture Canada. As well, the new Department will receive an additional 30 person years and $2.3 million in operating funds this year with an additional 30 to 45 person years in 1990. Forestry Canada this year has received $2.5 million in additional funding for research and development. This will increase by another $5 million next year. Forestry Canada has also received 37 person years for this year to help wind down the recently expired forestry agreements.
So there have been some significant numbers and person years not contained in the Main Estimates that are at work in the transition from Forestry Canada to the new department of forestry at this time. As I say, in terms of developing and broadening the influence, the scope and the impact of this department over future years in the subject areas that we have discussed on the Standing Committee on Forestry and Fisheries I see that it will grow in significant stature, influence and in the impact it will have on Canada's forestry sector and in the creation of our best example of sustainable development.
September 26, 1989

Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the comments of the member from Fredericton, who is also a member of the forestry committee, as well as to some of the earlier comments made by the member from Skeena, who I think has brought forward a very enlightened view about forestry from a biological perspective. His concerns that he certainly had both as a forestry critic and currently as our party's environment critic are well known.
I have two questions for the member. The first one concerns his wrap-up comments. He suggested that this Bill needs some work and that we are to do some studying for the flowering role that we anticipate from the department. In light of the fact that it has taken some five years for this government to finally introduce this legislation based on a commitment made during the 1984 election campaign, I am wondering if this government's definition of a flowering role is as immediate as the definition prior to that. Will it take five years for us to see that?
Second, I am interested in knowing the member's comments in terms of the representations that have been made to the committee and earlier when this legislation was introduced to the hon. government House Leader inquiring about the opportunity for the forest committee to have a chance to travel the country to hear Canadians' views on this legislation. The Canadian Institute of Forestry, which I believe is monitoring the debate today, has called for that. I wonder if the member from Fredericton would join with us in supporting that call from the CIF.

Mr. Speaker, with regard to the first question, this bill merely establishes the department of forestry. While I use the word "merely" I do so advisedly because it is in reality a very profound commitment, a very profound creation of a full-fledged federal government department. That must be accomplished before we can start to address the purposes that it will serve in the future. As I said earlier, Liberal governments over a period of almost 15 years dismantled the federal department of forestry which was established in 1960. This
Government Orders
government over the past five years has delivered on its commitment. It has delivered on its commitment to create a department of forestry.
That is the starting point we must have in order to pursue the purposes which the hon. member from Prince George has proposed and referred to subsequently, that being the opportunity for the standing committee to travel the country to hear from the Canadian Institute of Forestry and from the forestry sector broadly, to hear all who are interested in forestry and the environment, about the kinds of purposes which the federal department of forestry can ultimately fulfil. Yes, I would support such a mission by the Standing Committee on Forestry and Fisheries. I have already indicated I would support it.
In fact, I did inquire of the government, as we had committed to do, about the prospects of having this bill referred to the Standing Committee on Forestry and Fisheries. I have been advised that the government would prefer to see it dealt with in the normal legislative committee format that it has quickly offered to ensure that every member of the standing committee who wishes to participate on that legislative committee will be invited to do so. So I think we have delivered on the spirit of the undertakings which we unanimously agreed to in the Standing Committee on Forestry and Fisheries.
I would urge the House and particularly the members on the standing committee, to support the referral of this bill to a legislative committee and to support the passage of the bill as quickly as possible. Then let us take this new department of forestry and go on the road across Canada as a mission to determine how we can best use that department to influence sustainable development in forestry for the good of all Canadians.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mulroney that Bill C-29, an act to establish the Department of Forestry, to amend the Forestry Development and Research Act and to make related amendments to other acts, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I am especially pleased to have an opportunity to speak on Bill C-29, the government's bill to establish a department of forestry. I say to the minister, even though he is five years late that we support the initiative, albeit five years down the pipe. We think that forestry is the most important industry in the country, that a department of forestry, if it is adequately funded and provided for with the minister having control of all the factors relating to forestry, can have a tremendous impetus for good in this country. It is our number one industry. It is bigger than the petroleum industry. It is bigger than the automobile industry. It employs more people.
More important, Mr. Speaker, it is the key industry in many of the northern areas of this country where there is no chance, or very little chance, of establishing an automobile plant such as we have in southern Ontario. So it is an industry that is really on the move.
Through the 1970s and 1980s, when the Liberal government was in office, we put in place massive programs to upgrade. I think of my own constituency of Algoma where we provided some $25 million along with the province of Ontario to upgrade the Eddy Forest plant in Espanola to bring it into line with modem environmental demands. It increased efficiency and improved the productivity of that plant.
We provided assistance under the Department of Regional and Industrial Expansion to put in place the most productive sawmill at Naim Centre, part of the Eddy industry, which produces today over 200 million board-feet of lumber, an amount unheard of in eastern Canada only 25 years or so ago. It certainly has the largest productive capacity in eastern Canada.
September 26, 1989

Those programs were good. The several hundred million dollars which the former government put in place spawned investment by the private sector of $1.6 billion to modernize and update that industry. There is no question about the importance of this industry. What a tremendous contribution it makes in terms of jobs and technological development. The beauty is that it is a renewable resource. It is not like a mine where you dig the mineral out of the ground once and it is gone. If we properly husband the forest resources of our country; if we provide the research back-up, if we provide the tools for reforestation and research, it will continue to be the most important industry in our country, not only in jobs but export, balance of payments and so on.
This initiative of Bill C-29 can be very important and very productive. Unfortunately, if you look at this bill, look at the rhetoric of the Minister of Forestry, then look at the budget, and look at what the government has done in the past four years and how long it has taken them to do it, you cannot be sure of that. Some people in the industry say: "Look, when I am dealing with a trade problem, I want to deal with the Minister for International Trade. When I am dealing with a tax problem, I want to deal with the Minister of Finance". So, although the bill is there, the department will be there, it will only be effective if the minister has clout, if the minister has the power in the cabinet, if the minister has the influence of the Minister of Finance to ensure that things happen in this industry and if there is that over-all power to co-ordinate the activities that are necessary for the forest industry.
Let us just look at a few of these items. It is very unreassuring. I, along with the Member for Cochrane-Superior, and four or five other members of our caucus from northern Ontario, were members of a task force last winter which travelled across northern Ontario and talked to the forest industry. One segment of that industry, the softwood lumber industry, is in peril of being destroyed. It is a very important industry with tremendous resources in this country. We are very productive, we could compete with the world. Certainly, we can compete with the United States. It is in terrible jeopardy because it was a pawn in the free trade negotiations.
Government Orders
In December 1985, the government gave to the United States, as part of the negotiation of the free trade deal, an export tax that was not indexed to the value of the Canadian dollar. Therefore, that industry's exports to the United States have been reduced from 34 per cent of the American market to 26 per cent. Many plants in northern Ontario have shut down. Many are on short shift. Many having given up selling softwood lumber to the United States. The government has implemented other programs for transportation which have been very harmful to the industry. The industry is under at least a 30 to 35 per cent disadvantage from what it was before the export tax went into place.
We recommended to the minister that the export tax be renegotiated immediately so that that industry could continue to prosper, or if the government in the United States refuses to negotiate that they unilaterally rescind the tax and let the chips fall where they may. The industry is being wiped out in any event. If the Americans were to countervail, it probably would not be any worse than the existing situation which makes it almost impossible for northern Ontario mills to operate.
I was delighted and pleased because the Member for Cochrane-Superior drew to my attention a press clipping from the Ottawa Citizen of July 27 in which the Minister of Forestry said that the government was reviewing the 15 per cent export tax because it had just been pointed out to him that there were over 100 layoffs in Renfrew County alone as a result of this. Speaking about the Americans, the minister said that we will present them with a proposition to test the ground before we send them a termination notice. I am delighted that at least the minister has admitted that there is a big, serious problem with the export tax. It has caused layoffs in northern Ontario, and people have been laid off. It is causing serious problems right across the country. What we want to see is the minister either complete that negotiation or give the termination notice.
This is where we get back to the whole question of clout. The minister says this, and the minister is an honourable man. Even though he is not in the House this afternoon, he is still an honourable man and I am sure he means it. I suspect that if the minister goes to his friend, the Prime Minister, or to the Minister of International Trade and tells them that he is going to unilaterally terminate the export tax agreement, they will politely tell him to buzz off. I do not think the minister has the

Government Orders
clout to make that kind of decision. I hope he has, because I think that is the right move. Otherwise we are just knuckling under to the United States and our industry is being wiped out.
You can imagine what a reduction of 8 per cent of the United States market does, because that is a very vast market in the United States. It seems to me that we are big losers. I hope that the minister has the kind of clout that he needs to have a successful Department of Forestry and that he will move to remove that export tax because it is crippling northern Ontario.
The second area where I see that the whole question of strength and prestige of the minister is important is in the forestry agreements. For the past five years, we have had a forestry agreement in the province of Ontario, $150 million, shared by the two levels of government, designed to carry out the necessary reforestation and the necessary research to provide for sustainable development in the production and reforestation of our province.
Regardless of how gloriously the minister talks about these agreements, he has not been able to get the money to reinstate them. That is literally a tragedy. It is not just a tragedy for five years, or ten, or fifteen years. It is a tragedy into the future because it is important that those forestry agreements be maintained.
If we look at the arrangements, we cannot be confident that we are going to have a department and a minister with the necessary clout. For those forestry agreements, the funding comes down through the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion from the ACOA agreement and the Western Diversification Agreement and it just does not seem that the minister is in control. If he were, then those forestry agreements and the funding would be coming directly from his department and not through the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion.
In Ontario we have the FEDNOR agreement and the funding there comes from the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. We are told that the assistant deputy minister for that department is not even located in Ontario. He is located in Montreal in the province of Quebec.
Yet we have, in Sault Ste. Marie, the Great Lakes Forest Research Laboratory, one of the largest institutions in the country for research and the implementation of the Forestry Agreement is carried out from that laboratory. Surely we want the co-ordination for those agreements to be coming from the Minister of Forestry and not coming down through the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion.
If we look at the minister's funding, last year when the government brought in its spending estimates in the budget, it was indicated that the government would be spending in the 1988-89 fiscal year $9.9 billion, the largest budget in the history of Canada as far as the federal budget of $142.9 billion is concerned. There was an increase there of $9.9 billion dollars across the country. Yet, if we look at the Department of Forestry we see a decrease of $28 million.
That does not give anyone confidence that the creation of a Department of Forestry is going to be very powerful. If you remove the funding, regardless of all the names and all the rhetoric from the minister, but do not actually provide additional funding, or do not even give the minister the power to establish the forestry agreements, which, after all, are the agreements which really touch the forests and result in trees being planted, and new hybrid breeds being developed that touch on the whole forest industry and if they are all controlled by the minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, the minister responsible for ACOA, or the minister responsible for Western Diversification, it does not sound as if the minister has much ability to co-ordinate the activities of the department.
We are not only talking about a reduction in the forestry agreements. We are not only talking about a reduction in the budget of the Department of Forestry. We are talking about a reduction in the number of person years, a reduction of 47 person years. It does not sound like a department that is going anywhere if it is being reduced in the number of person years. Regardless of how fancy are the names we give it as a new Department of Forestry, which we are all pleased to see, we want to see the cash. You cannot really be effective unless you have the funds to carry out the responsibility.
September 26, 1989

Forestry has gone down by some 11.9 per cent in its budget. At the same time, other resource related departments, for example, Energy, Mines and Resources, has gone up by 22.9, almost double. It has gone up by twice as much as the Department of Forestry has gone down.
We are pleased to see a Department of Forestry created. We would certainly like to see a strong department with a minister with clout, to not only do the things that need to be done for this industry, but to co-ordinate what is going on already. Otherwise, we will be going over to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion to find out what he is planning to do with the department and with these forestry agreements.
What we are concerned about is the government's attitude with regard to ERDA agreements-economic and regional development agreements-and that we are gradually going to be seeing a winnowing down. We will have a minister of departmental status and all this, but he will essentially be a little secretariat effectively running six labs across the country. That is not what we want. We want a minister who controls forestry agreements, controls the labs, has influence in cabinet, has influence on decisions with regard to finance, with regard to matters relating to export trade and with regard to manpower and research. There is simply no evidence that this is what we are going to get with the creation of this department.
First of all, it has taken five years to create it and it is not created yet. All the decisions with regard to export tax, forestry agreements, budget, and manpower, militate against this. We support the bill. We hope that it will be beneficial, but we want to see action. We want to see the government put its money where its mouth is. This is a key industry for us. It provides opportunities for our country in many different ways and it should be supported more than it has been by this government for the last four years.

speechtext: On questions and comments, the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague from Algoma had some serious things to say and I think he delivered them in a serious manner. I have to take exception to some of his comments, but I would like to mention a couple of comments right off the bat. He talked about the government attitude. I was in the forest industry for many years and I can tell you that the government attitude over the last four years has been a one thousand per cent improvement over what it was formerly. There have been many things done in co-operation with industry and with the provinces.

Government Orders
Some of his colleagues this morning, when talking about the forestry bill, said that the first thing they want to do is bring inspectors into the provinces as policemen to enforce what they think should be done with industry and the provinces. It is exactly that kind of action which created such a problem in prior years with the provinces and with the industry.
A typical answer-and I am distressed by it-is that they seem to want to dictate from Ottawa what the solutions are and then they want to take all the money they can and throw it up against the wall and see if it will stick. Their concrete suggestions so far are to throw more money at the bill. Have they not been listening to the people in Canada and what they have been saying? They are saying: "Please, government, don't spend more money unnecessarily."
There is nothing wrong with trying to achieve excellence, even in government. A small, trim, efficient forestry department can do far more than an inefficient, large government bureaucracy. They should be taking their energies, their expertise, and leading this nation in the forest industry. They can do that. The dollars should primarily come from industry and from the provinces where most of the benefit goes. What it requires is a co-operative government and leadership.
The point that I have to-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: This is questions and comments.

I have a question about free trade. He said in December 1985,that this government, as part of its free trade negotiations, gave away the memorandum of understanding. That is absolutely and totally incorrect.
I was one of the forestry executives who heard about the collaboration between industry, provincial governments, and the federal government. The industry spent millions of dollars lobbying Ottawa. It recognized the threat to the forest industry with the countervail. In fact, when it was finally resolved, the Conservative government went to the industry and said: "What shall we do? These are the options." It was industry that said: "We
have to accept." It was our unions that said: "Yes, we have to accept." And it was our provincial governments that said: "Yes, we have to accept that. The deal that we can get there is better than the other options."
I would like to know why, in spite of the facts, you misrepresent so terribly the actual situations of the free trade deal and the memorandum of understanding.

I would be delighted to respond to the hon. member for Cariboo-Chilcotin. I had a telex from the vice-president of the Canadian Forest Industries Council in December, 1986-1 am sorry I said 1985, it was actually in 1986-in which they totally denounce the cave-in of the Government of Canada on the export tax. The industry is variously represented to have spent between $4 million and $10 million fighting the United States countervail threat, as they did in 1982. They are absolutely opposed-and I do not know who he talked to, unless it was some of his Tory friends-to the cave-in which the government did on that agreement. Clearly the industry was opposed to the government knuckling under. If the United States had imposed the countervail duty, it had every opportunity at the International Trade Court or under the GATT to oppose it and would have done so successfully.
Now we are left with an industry which is in terrible straits, at least in northern Ontario. It is my understanding that the level of the stumpage charge is extremely heavy for that industry to carry in B.C. In my opinion, the government knuckled under because the Prime Minister was so hell-bent on getting a free trade deal that he would agree to anything with the Americans.
The member talks about funding, throwing money at a problem. What all of the provinces are asking and all the industry is asking the federal government to do is to continue the federal-provincial forestry agreements that they have had for the past five years. The federal government is unilaterally wiping them out so that the kind of reforestation that needs to take place, the kind of research that needs to take place, is simply not going to occur. I think that that is a tragedy. It is a tragedy for areas like mine in northern Ontario. It is a tragedy, I am sure, for many areas in B.C. and I do not see that as interference.
September 26, 1989

I have met with federal and provincial people. The management teams that have been put together on those forestry agreements imply no unreasonable interference. It is a co-operative operation in any event. The federal government generally has the laboratory and research capacity more in its bailiwick, or at least in Ontario it has a great deal. They have combined in places like Sault Ste. Marie at the Great Lakes Forest Research Laboratory. They have the MNR labs there now.
It is a case of the federal government abandoning those forestry agreements, cutting the provinces adrift, and short-changing the whole industry now, but more important, short-changing the industry for that research in the future because research is a long horizon. We have to do it now if we want the results at the end of the term, whether it is five years or 10 years.
I completely reject the member's comments in that regard from my experience. We want to see this bill passed, but we want to see the wherewithal dedicated whether it is from External Affairs, going to the proper minister, the Minister of Forestry.

I have a question for the Hon. Member for Algoma. He chastises the government for not previously establishing a forestry industry, something which I am in agreement with, but also indicates his strong support and the support of his colleagues for beefing up a separate Department of Forestry, putting some teeth into it, giving it some clout. I want to remind the hon. member that on August 1, 1984, in Prince George, his leader, the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra, in fact, outrightly rejected the concept of a separate forest ministry. In large bold print in the Prince George Citizen it stated: "Turner rejects forestry ministry". I would like to ask the member, in view of the past position of his Party and his leader-

I would like to bring to the attention of the hon. member that he is now on debate. There are no more questions or comments. I will allow this short question. The hon. member's time has expired as far as questions and comments are concerned and I was giving the floor on debate to the

I would like to ask the hon. member, in light of this information, why he and his colleagues decided to do this flip-flop on the issue. I am sure they do not want to be charged as being guilty of political opportunism.

As I said, I think it is important just what commitment the government has. The government has no commitment to the industry, as it has shown with the export tax of 15 per cent, which is decimating the industry. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Okanagan-Shuswap on debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am going to rise to support the general principle of the bill although I believe, as do my colleagues, that there needs to be a number of amendments made. It does have a few inconsistencies, a few weaknesses, a few warts.

Government Orders
We will be making a number of these amendments and this will be outlined at a later stage of debate by my colleague, the member for Prince George.
I would like to say that over the years the responsibility for forests has been shuffled in and out of, I think, nine different departments to where it currently resides in the Department of Agriculture. That seems to be a rather strange place to tuck a responsibility that has as its mandate the largest industry right across this country. I think as a result of this there has been a lack of continuity in direction.
Back in 1984 the Prime Minister had proposed some strong support for forestry but it took an awful long time for this government to finally come to its senses to realize the critical situation that our major industry in Canada was facing. To understand and address some of those priorities we needed to develop a separate ministry. I think it is something that is long overdue. We support the spirit of the legislation and we believe that we do need a strengthened department of forestry that can address some of the serious concerns affecting this industry.
I believe that we need strong leadership in a number of areas, such as regional forest resource development, national forestry research in pollution control, in wildlife conservation and in parks and recreation. I do believe that by strengthening and developing a separate ministry for forests, a separate department of forests that we can go a. long way toward realizing those goals.
However, what does concern me somewhat is in order to do that you also need to strengthen the level of funding for the department. What concerns me is that we have seen a department created without the financial clout necessary to do the job.
As a matter of fact, in 1989-90 we will be seeing funds available for regional forestry programs actually reduced by the sum of about $24 million. It appears those will now be funnelled not directly into the Forestry Resource Development Agreements, the FRDAs, but through the Western Diversification Programs making, I believe by extension of the argument, even less money available for those extremely important reforestation programs, not only in western Canada, but throughout this country.
I would like to turn to the FRDA agreements for a moment and talk about some of their impacts generally, specifically referring to British Columbia and my area of B.C. which is in the Okanagan-Shuswap.
Historically, the FRDA agreements were negotiated with the provinces because of the recognition that our forests across Canada needed on-going management in order to sustain and to increase our forest resources. Those agreements were started about five years ago and a number of them were signed with provinces across Canada. Six of them have now expired, and many of those have not been renewed.
In British Columbia we still do have an active FRDA program but it does expire in March of 1990. The B.C. government and the forestry industry is looking for a significant increase in funding to these programs which is currently at a level of about $300 million.
If you go back to the Pearse report of a few years back, Dr. Peter Pearse, Resource Economist from the University of British Columbia, in fact stressed that the need for funding for forest renewal was much, much greater than that. There is significant reason for us not to be cutting back on the funding for reforestation programs but to be extending it. Now we see that funding source being depleted. A $24-million cut for the western provinces and funnelled through western diversification. Now it seems that the minister of forestry is going to have to go cap in hand to the minister responsible for regional economic development to try to obtain funding for those very important agreements. We do not believe that to be correct. We believe that those agreements need the full level of funding that has presently been committed in order to sustain the amount of work that has already gone on in restocking those NSR lands, those not sufficiently restocked forest lands. To cut back on those agreements at this point is going to endanger the work that has in fact already been done.
With a strengthened department of forests which this legislation suggests, we have a lot of opportunity to strengthen those kinds of reforestation programs. What concerns us is that although we have created this department, the commitment to the FRDA programs for reforestation does not seem to be there.
Let us consider what is at stake if these programs are cut back or if they are cancelled. British Columbia provides over half of Canada's softwood lumber. We have about $13 billion per year in shipments of forest products from the province. That amounts to about
247,000	direct and indirect jobs, supporting 126 communities. Those are 1988 figures. That amounts to about $530 million of tax revenue to Ottawa. We in British Columbia are already experiencing, and have for some time, a fall down in our annual allowable cut because we are simply running out of mature timber to harvest.

Government Orders
We have seen the closure of mills in my constituency and in a number of other areas throughout the province. Fletcher Challenge in Lumby and in a number of other areas in the province has closed its operations. Why? The reason it says is: "Gosh guys, we just do not have enough good timber available to us. We are running out of timber."
The reforestation programs through the FRDA agreements have the mandate to replenish those timber supplies so that we can lessen the fall down in the future. If we cut back on those FRDA agreements at this point, that program is jeopardized, future jobs are jeopardized in British Columbia and, in fact, right across Canada.
In addition, when we experience a significant fall down in our annual allowable cut, whether it be in the Okanagan or anywhere in the province, the Government of Canada experiences a significant decline in its taxation revenues. We should consider that in terms of setting economic priorities.
The importance of FRDAs to British Columbia, of course, is essentially for the protection and preservation of our forest resources not now, but for future generations, so that in 10, 20, 50 or 80 years' time we still have trees to cut, we still have jobs for people to go to. That will be supported by tree planting now, by weeding and thinning programs, by forestry research and by using integrated methods of resource management that are available through those forest resource development agreements.
I would like to turn to the concept of forest management. This is something I think that this strengthened department of forestry could well look at in terms of strengthening its mandate and some of its priorities, at least in British Columbia. There is the control and growth of alder and aspen trees in regenerating areas that have been disturbed by harvesting, and the planting of trees that are valuable as commercial species, such as Douglas fir and western hemlock. These are elements of the reforestation program that are so vital through the FRDA agreements.
If those agreements are cut back or perhaps, God forbid, cancelled, the work that has gone on over the past five years will be wasted.
I took the opportunity to see a number of FRDA programs in my area in the Okanagan. We toured with a number of forestry and local political officials and saw the kind of work that has been done in our area respecting the provincial-federal FRDA agreement. I must say that I think all of us were duly impressed with the kind of regeneration taking place in those NSR lands.
That program for regeneration has to be nurtured over the next 15 to 20 years to ensure that those seedlings are able to grow into a mature forest. If we were to cancel those programs now the overgrowth of alder and deciduous plants would simply wipe out many of the seedlings that are now healthy and viable plants growing into our future forest products.
It is very critical that we continue to nurture these FRDA programs through the injection of federal funds and through the injection of provincial funds to ensure that the groundwork that we have laid over the past five years does not simply vanish. What a false economy that would be: $300 million dollars of federal investment would be simply wasted if those programs are jeopardized.
In British Columbia, before the FRDA agreement with B.C. was signed around 1985, there were approximately 738,000 hectares of land that qualified as NSR land. This land was lying fallow. It was not sufficiently restocked and had been logged over.
I fly over much of the province many times during the course of the year. I am continually amazed as I fly back and forth over our province of British Columbia, a province that is responsible for half the annual harvest in this country, at the amount of land that lies clear cut, eroding and bare, the top soil being washed away.
I am not sure how accurate it is- I would assume that it would be well within range-but somebody estimated that the NSR lands currently in our province amount to a 200 mile strip that is 50 miles wide. That is a strip 50 miles wide extending from Vancouver all the way past the city of Penticton in the Okanagan. That is the significant damage done to our resource in the past years

September 26, 1989
Government Orders
without a proper restocking program. I submit that these FRDA programs are chipping away at that. We have in the past five years reduced that backlog by some 185,000 hectares. We are making gains and slowly recovering those NSR lands, putting them into production for future harvesting programs. But it is going to take time. It is going to take a long-term financial commitment from this government, one that I am afraid this government no longer sees as being a major priority.
I submit, once again, that we are developing a strengthened department of forestry with this legislation. Along with that we should be making the kinds of financial commitments we must make to ensure the future of our forests in B.C. and in Canada to ensure the future of our industry and to ensure the future of jobs for Canadians.
In terms of British Columbians, the FRDA programs have allowed 500 permanent jobs and 15,000 short-term jobs to be created. Our sustainable harvest, since the development of those programs, has increased by some
600,000	cubic meters each year.
We have had an increase in our Gross Domestic Product of about $56 million a year, and also an increased habitat for wildlife. They are valuable programs. We need the continued funding. Let us not give up on them now.
I want to talk for a moment specifically about the FRDA as it applies to the Okanagan-Shuswap. It is part of the interior British Columbia that my constituency is located in, and the Okanagan-Shuswap is part of the Kamloops forest district. We have a regional total of about 6.7 million hectares, an area that is larger than Nova Scotia.
The Shuswap-Okanagan Forestry Association has been calling for some time now for a commitment, both federally and provincially, to replenish the fall down in the timber supplies through tackling the NSR lands and developing the appropriate reforestation and silviculture programs that we now see through the current FRDA agreements.
During that FRDA tour that I was talking about in regard to my area, there were a number of sites that we looked at. We went to about five through the Lumby, Enderby and Vernon areas. Those five sites indicate the
kinds of problems that the Shuswap-Okanagan Forestry Association had been and still is talking about, including the need to replenish our forest stocks. We saw the impact of the FRDA agreements in terms of the kind of work that is being done. We saw the results of the research, the silviculture programs, the weeding and thinning programs.
Those programs are successfully reducing that backlog of NSR lands in our area. People are proud of that. People want to see it continued. The Shuswap-Okanagan Forestry Association wants to see it continued. The forestry companies throughout the Okanagan want to see it continued. They want to practise responsible forest management. We need that financial commitment and we need to maintain it over the next decade, over the next 20 or 30 years to ensure that those goals are met.
I think a strengthened department of forestry can be mandated to look at environmental initiatives that are required in forest management: wildlife conservation, the development of parks and recreation areas. I think that a strengthened department of forestry is going to need to provide real leadership in this area and in areas of habitat conservation, and particularly in areas of resource management conflicts.
Out in British Columbia we have had ongoing problems for some time, largely because of the actions of our provincial government over the past 20-odd years, and partially as a result of the failure of both the federal and provincial governments at resolving some of our native land settlement claims. Areas like the Carmanah, the Stein, and the Stikine,. We all know that South Moresby, the Spatsizi Plateau, and the Kutzimateen are all areas, that, if not actively under contention in terms of resource-used conflict, will be in the future.
It is important that a strengthened ministry of forestry be mandated to work co-operatively with the provincial governments at trying to overcome some of these problem areas. I think it is clearly evident, given the importance of the forestry industry to the Canadian economy, that the prime mandate of a federal department of forestry should be to provide leadership in the areas that are impacted by our forest resource so that we can maintain this resource, so that we can protect it and replenish it for future generations.
September 26, 1989

I support this bill. I must admit that it has weaknesses and my colleague from Prince George-Bulkley Valley will be making a number of very wise and judicious amendments at a later time that will, hopefully, strengthen many of those weaknesses. The bill does not satisfy all the concerns.
It needs substantial amendment but it is a start, and based upon our long-term commitment as New Democrats for the development of a strong forestry ministry at the federal level, we are going to be supporting this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment the hon. member for Okanagan-Shuswap for his support of this bill and I would assume that he would join with me in commending and complimenting the Minister of State for Forestry for the leadership and initiative that he has shown in bringing this bill before the House.
I do want to raise a question and perhaps I misunderstood but I do have a great deal of interest in forestry because included within my own South Shore constituency is Queen's County, Nova Scotia, which, as you may know, is known as the forestry capital of Canada.
I want to raise the question of FRDAs. We are very pleased in Atlantic Canada with the success that we have recently achieved with the signing of two very significant Forest Resource Development Agreements, one a $45 million agreement announced last Friday by the minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, and a $91 million agreement announced for the province of New Brunswick.
It has been our experience in Atlantic Canada that these FRDAs have worked extremely well. One of the reasons they have worked well is that the provinces themselves identify the priorities within resource development areas. It is clear that in Atlantic Canada forestry is recognized as a major area for economic development and it is a major priority with our provincial governments but it is also a priority that has, and I think quite properly, been recognized by this government.
Government Orders
There was some discussion about the length of time taken to reach the agreements, but I think it is important to note that right at the beginning of the process the minister made it clear that there would be new forest resource development agreements. Again, I commend him. That was very helpful to us, unlike, I might say, in 1982 under the previous government when the last agreements expired and there was no indication as to whether there would be new agreements. As a result, people were laid off and we lost some very valuable people in our industry. That has not happened this time because the minister made it clear right from the beginning that there would be agreements. I think the process works extremely well and I would like to compliment the government on it.
Perhaps I misunderstood my friend opposite but I assume that he also supports this very valuable initiative in the way the federal and provincial governments work together. I assume again that he is joining with me in commending the minister of forestry for his initiative in bringing forward this excellent bill.

Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. colleague had mentioned that Nova Scotia had received about $91 million in terms of the renewed FRDA and I am pleased for Nova Scotia that it did receive that commitment. I want to point out that Nova Scotia is, in fact, smaller in terms of land mass than the Kamloops forest district.
If you break the regional or provincial FRDA for B.C. down, which is $300 million, the appropriated amount for the Kamloops area, the interior, was only $30 million. If we are looking at $30 million for an area that is in fact larger than what the member opposite is indicating for Nova Scotia, which has $91 million. I would submit that in the interest of regional equity the member would support my suggestion that the FRDA for British Columbia be at least tripled.
Hear, hear!

He mentioned them himself, for which I thank him, and I just ask my colleague for the good of forestry in Canada to support the Bill, to support the Minister's negotiations and to let British Columbia, like any other Canadian province, benefit from these agreements and share the benefits with its people.

Just to clarify, Mr. Speaker, the constituency is Okanagan-Shuswap. I thank the member opposite for his remarks, but I suggest to the member that you can conclude all the agreements you want to, but if the funding is not there, the agreements are not worth very much.
With the funding being allocated through western diversification, I submit that the minister is going to have to go cap in hand to the minister responsible for the appropriation of funding through western diversification to ask if the money is available. In addition to that, there is $24 million less going into western diversification, it is my understanding, for this fiscal year than there was before. I submit to you that if the pie is getting smaller and it is divided into more pieces nobody will get more or a larger piece of the pie. I do not know what that means in terms of the forestry resource agreements out west. That is what we are concerned about.
