moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should refuse funding to groups that are actively working against women's equality as guaranteed in The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and in international agreements signed by Canada, such as the Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Discrimination Against Women.

She said: Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak to a motion that I am introducing before my colleagues in the House, and I will read it again even though you have read it:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should refuse funding to groups that are actively working against women's equality as guaranteed in The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and in international agreements signed by Canada, such as the Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Discrimination Against Women.
I am distressed that I have cause to bring this motion forward. It really seems unbelievable that it is up to a private member of this House to have to inform the government that women's equality must be worked for and not undermined. In this day and age, one would expect that the Government of Canada would not be actively using its financial resources against equality for women.
I am referring to a particular incident in which this government used funds that are reserved for equalityseeking women's groups. The government granted $21,212 to REAL Women for a conference it held last April. This group has over the years opposed many rights the women of Canada have been fighting hard for. My motion is directed against any further funding to groups that work against women's equality. I will explain why it is important to refuse funds to such groups, and I will use last April's incident as an example.
It is evident to me that the government tried to hide its funding decision from the public and from interested members of Parliament. I tried to get the co-operation of the office of the Secretary of State which granted this funding to answer basic questions about the process and the reasons the decisions were made.
The Secretary of State's office gave me the runaround. They gave us phone numbers of people to call, people who told us nothing but who simply referred us back to the Secretary of State's office. This office refused to discuss the funding, saying only that the decision was consistent with women's program funding guidelines, but even the briefest look at women's program funding guidelines will tell anyone that this group did not conform to the guidelines. In fact, it is because this group does not conform to the guidelines that it was repeatedly refused women's program funding in the past.
Government Orders
I had to do what I did next because my efforts in dealing with this Secretary of State's office as a member of Parliament were really completely fruitless. I applied as a private citizen under the Access to Information law to obtain the necessary documents that would allow me to see how this decision could possibly have been made. I paid the fee and I filled out the forms. Every effort was made to stall my request. The Secretary of State had a thirty day deadline to respond to my request. It asked for an extension.
I finally received the document only a few days before the conference in question was due to take place. The process I had to undergo to obtain basic information about that funding decision was really shameful. The public has a right to know that its money is being used inappropriately, that its money is being utilized to undermine the hard earned rights women have won over the past century.
The report I received of this government-funded conference told me that in one workshop, the credibility of every female Supreme Court justice was questioned simply because they were women. Madam Justice Bertha Wilson, an experienced and respected judge, was touted as an example of the affirmative action gone awry.
People who think women are incompetent are certainly entitled to their opinion, I suppose, but to have the Government of Canada paying for such a forum in the name of equality is outrageous. It is absolutely outrageous.
Another workshop funded by the Canadian government in the name of equality for women was one in which a male psychiatrist claimed that children in child care would grow up to be partial psychopaths. It is really difficult to see how this statement, which has absolutely no credibility, has anything to do with the equality of women.
Also, in the child care workshop, the audience was told by the workshop leader that women must be nurturers because of their potential to breastfeed. The Conservative government, in defending this funding on the basis that it did meet equality criteria, obviously does not have the first clue as to what equality really means. I will endeavour to explain it.

Government Orders
A part of equality is that men and women have the freedom to do what they, as individuals, are best at and what they wish to do. Many women in a free and equal society will choose to nurture small children; some women will choose not to do this. Many men are capable of nurturing and helping children grow into well balanced, responsible adults.
Women should not be forced into nurturing, nor should men be forced away from it. That is not equality nor is it reasonable or realistic. Why does the government defend rigid sex role stereotyping as a different perspective on equality? It has nothing at all to do with equality.
Another workshop leader in a workshop on pornography said that universal day care would lead to a greater pornography problem because of working mothers. First, I would like to clarify for the government and for anti-equality groups that every mother is a working mother. Raising children is work. Second, I would like to explain to the government that pinning the ills of society on women who work outside the home is an abdication of our collective responsibility to deal with social problems in our country.
In the 1800s, movements arose to deal with society's problems. These were slavery, child labour, extreme poverty and exploitation, high illiteracy, high infant mortality and alcoholism among others.
Some of our social problems have changed. However, the fact remains that we must continue to organize ourselves into progressive movements for change such as the women's movement. We cannot sit back and blame one particular group in our society such as women in the paid labour force for all that is wrong in our world today. Not only is that terribly unfair but it is really not at all useful.
I ask myself why this government is defending its funding of workshops which claim that everything bad is the fault of women in the paid labour force, saying that this is equality. Blaming women is not equality. It is anti-equality.
There was a workshop on the United Nations Charter of Equality for Women to which Canada is a signatory. The essence of the workshop was that the charter was not in favour of "true equality" because it encouraged women to participate in the paid work force.
Another theme of the conference was hatred, lies and intolerance of homosexuality. Again, is this somehow connected with women's equality? The government was unable to explain how out and out lies about lesbians and about gay men are related to furthering equality for women. Yet this government paid for it to be said and paid for it to be promoted.
The conference was openly anti-feminist. One workshop leader told her audience that she hoped REAL Women will be able to counter the effects of the feminist movement. Again, the government stood by its decision to fund this conference dedicated to countering the effects of the women's movement.
The effects of the feminist movement, for the record, include women's right to vote, a married woman's right to own property, the right not to be sexually harassed in the workplace, the right not to be sexually harassed by a stranger, by an acquaintance or by a husband, the right to be included in the Constitution as a free and equal being, equal wages for equal work, and the right to disseminate information about birth control. That right was illegal before 1969. These are the proud achievements of the women's movement over the past century in Canada.
Today the women's movement is fighting for homemakers' pensions, for equal pay for work of equal value, for an end to the economic barriers that all women face, for good quality child care and for women's rights to control their own bodies and their own lives. The women's movement has not only lobbied for these rights but continues to provide services for women, services which include information, counselling for abused women, self-defence courses and support for pregnant women and for new mothers. These are the groups from which the Secretary of State has withdrawn funding to give to an anti-equality group.
October 18 is the sixtieth anniversary of Persons' Day. This is the day that women officially became persons in Canada, thanks to the efforts of many women but especially of Nellie McClung, Emily Murphy, Henrietta Muir Edwards, Louise McKinney and Irene Parlby. Sixty years after women obtained legal status as persons in Canada, our government is funding groups that want to turn back the clock, groups which are afraid of the future.
September 26, 1989

It is understandable that people fear change. It is confusing to many people when they are no longer faced with rigid sex stereotypical roles. They are unsure of what to do or how it is that they should behave. Women at home are justifiably claiming their right to respect and recognition for the valuable work that they do. I worked at home long before I became a politician and I know what it is to raise three children on one income and to try to make ends meet. I cannot advocate a step backward in time, giving up rights that I and so many women before me have fought for and won.
I believe in a woman's right to choose, to choose whether she will raise children at home, whether she will enter the paid workforce, to choose what to do with her life and with her body. These are the ideas that the women's program is supposed to promote; positive, forward-looking strategies so that women and men may have more choices about their own lives.
This issue of choice is an important one in this debate. I have here a memo from the Secretary of State to the Vancouver Status of Women, one of the many valuable organizations whose funding has already been cut, concerning funding of a particular position on abortion. I will read it into the record.
Just a quick reminder that Secretary of State Department funding may not be used for any activity which takes a position on the issue of abortion.
This does not, of course, preclude your organization from forming, holding or sharing an opinion, belief or point of view, or taking action if it so wishes. Rather, this requires that these be done with funding other than that provided by Secretary of State Department.
To avoid any problems with current or planned activities, I again ask each organization to ensure that it understands and adheres to this policy. I would also ask each organization to ensure that if any activities are undertaken, your organization is certain it can clearly and unequivocably demonstrate that resources other than Secretary of State funding are used.
Vancouver Status of Women is a women's group which provides information and other services for women and is pro choice. REAL Women is a self-proclaimed prolife group. Vancouver Status of Women and all equalityseeking women's groups are prevented from using Secretary of State money to promote a point of view on abortion. Yet Secretary of State has funded an anti-abortion workshop at the REAL Women's conference.
Government Orders
At the conference, a workshop was led on anti-choice interventions at the Supreme Court level. I want to know, did Secretary of State make REAL Women clearly and uneqivocably demonstrate that resources other than Secretary of State funding were used to print up the materials which were used in the workshop or any posters that mentioned the workshop?
Why is it that the Secretary of State is applying a stricter standard to equality-seeking groups than to anti-equality groups? Why is it that the Secretary of State is clamping down on pro-choice groups in favour of anti-choice groups? Is this to promote the government's view on the abortion question, that we should have an ineffective law to restrict abortion but do nothing to help mothers or do anything to reduce the number of unwanted pregnancies? Is this part of a cohesive government strategy to silence pro-choice groups while promoting anti-choice groups?
I note that it is taking Revenue Canada a year to decide on the charitable tax status of the Eveiywoman's Health Clinic which provides a range of medical and counselling services including abortion. A group called Human Life International already has charitable tax status with Revenue Canada. This is the organization that sent horrific postcards to all members of Parliament. It showed decapitated foetus heads dripping with blood. The same group sent MPs a series of anti-choice articles as well as anti-child care article entitled "Daycareism and Socialism in Sweden".
Why is Secretary of State withdrawing a significant amount of funds for equality-seeking groups and at the same time granting new funds to anti-equality groups? What is this government's agenda for the women of Canada?
A curious thing about this whole incident of funding an anti-equality group is that it shows how very little power the minister responsible for the status of women seems to have in determining the government's policy on women. When I questioned her in committee, she did not wholeheartedly support this funding. Yet I have copies of letters written from the Secretary of State's office to outraged women's groups which wrote to the minister to complain of anti-equality funding. These letters say that the decision to fund REAL women was completely consistent with the women's program equality criteria.

September 26, 1989
Government Orders
It is difficult to argue with the minister who clearly does not understand what equality means. More to the point, what is evident is that the minister responsible for the status of women, who has a better idea of what equality means, was either not informed of the funding or was not listened to when she explained that such a conference did not promote equality for women.
One argument I have heard in favour of funding anti-equality groups is that they present a different perspective and that all perspectives must be respected. However, the mandate of the Secretary of State's women's program is not to fund womens' organizations, it is to fund equality-seeking womens' organizations.
The Secretary of State's complete disregard of the women's program guidelines leaves the door open to all sorts of really bizarre funding decisions. If the government is going to override its own guidelines and fund anti-equality groups, what will it fund next through the women's program, apolitical women's organization such as bowling leagues, the ladies auxiliary at the Ku Klux Klan? Who else is going to receive money previously earmarked for groups promoting equality between women and men in our society?
This government should really be ashamed of itself. It can no longer even pretend to support the equality of women in our society. It is imperative that this House support the motion to refuse funding to groups that are actively working against women's equality.
The women's program was a victim of the last budget in April. It was cut by 15 per cent. I received letters from every region of Canada. These letters expressed shock at this attack on an already under-funded program and under-funded groups. These groups have served women and communities across Canada on shoe string budgets. These women's groups often provide a service that the government would have to pay a lot more for if their functions were to be taken over by the government.

speakeroldname: Mr. Patrick Boyer (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the second day that Parliament is back in the fall session and we have before us a motion that shows clearly to the House and the country the line of reasoning and the kind of thinking for which members of the New Democratic Party are famous, for which reason all of us can be
thankful that they remain in opposition and have no prospect of forming the government. A fundamental principle of this country is the rule of law, not the rule according to the whim and subjective judgment of individuals.
What we are talking about here are criteria that are set out under which groups in this country can apply for funding. If they meet those criteria, they receive the funding. To say that beyond that there should be bureaucrats, politicians or others who can look in detail at what is said at a particular conference and, on the basis of that, should not allow the grants to go forward when those groups have met the qualifications is to say that the rules and the criteria are not applicable. This is, in effect, another face of the same question of universality which always has members of that party up on their hind legs barking. It is saying that when there are criteria established for grants then all who meet those criteria universally qualify.
Let me give an example of what the problem is with this subjective approach the New Democratic Party is now putting before us this afternoon. In 1985, I was chairing a committee of the House, the Parliamentary Committee on Equality Rights, made up of members of all three parties. We held hearings across the country and we held hearings in the city of Toronto at a downtown Toronto hotel. While we were in the process of holding our hearings, elsewhere in that same hotel NAC convened a press conference to condemn the process by which we were proceeding, to make criticisms of our committee and to generally take a great opportunity for grabbing some headlines through a petulant outburst that I thought was quite unwarranted.
The fact is that a few months later, a report was tabled entitled Equality for All. It contained 75 recommendations unanimously supported by all three parties, recommendations dealing with the equality of women, maternity benefits, armed forces, immigrant women, health issues relevant to women and so on. If I was taking the subjective standard of the member opposite, I would have said that NAC, using money provided by the federal government to launch that criticism of our committee and its workings, was at that time working against the interests of women's equality. That is exactly the reason that we do have rules that set those criteria and we do not indulge in the kind of subjective approach that is being taken here.
September 26, 1989

Another example is the Ontario case of election financing being provided to all political parties which registered. The Communist party registered in Ontario and qualified under the Election Finance Reform Act of Ontario for public funding. A lot of people in Ontario did not like the fact that their tax dollars were going to fund the Communist party. However, the same point applies. Because it met the criteria, it qualified for the funding and it received it. It was not up to government officials or bureaucrats to get subjectively involved and say: "No, only these main-line political parties will qualify and we do not like the smell of the Communist party. We do not like what they stand for, and therefore, they are not going to get the funding". No, if you set up the rules, they apply to everybody. Either you fund all the groups or you do not fund any of them.

Mr. Speaker, I would also like to say a few words about our Government's record on women's equality.
Our Government has every reason to be proud of what it has done to improve the status of women.
For instance, we could look at our Employment Equity Act, the steps we have taken to fight family violence and sexual exploitation of children, our announcement that we intend to increase parental and maternity benefits, the measures we took to ensure that alimony and custody orders are carried out and our decision to improve training opportunities for women.
We have developed programs to encourage women entrepreneurs. We have taken steps to help women farmers and we have opened all trades and professions in the Armed Forces to women.
In co-operation with the provinces, we have looked at women's training needs and their health concerns, and we have also looked into better ways of harmonizing women's work and family responsibilities. Our Government has appointed a record number of women in key positions in federal departments and agencies, the judiciary and the diplomatic corps.
All these achievements are irrefutable proof of our commitment to improving the status of women in all sectors of Canadian society. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, these achievements were the result of a joint effort. In all its initiatives to enhance the status of women, our Government sought the active of participation of the
Government Orders
provinces and territories, business and labour, the volunteer sector and, more importantly, women themselves, whether in groups or as individuals.
Our Government is very conscious of the remarkable contribution of women's groups to the development of our country.
As pioneers, women cleared land, established families and communities and took an active part in developing the country's social, economic, political and legal structures. They found their place in factories, offices, hospitals and schools, doing their share to strengthen and expand the Canadian economy. Today, women in increasing numbers are playing this essential role in our society.
Today, as in the past, despite all their domestic and family responsibilities, their careers and community involvement, women still find the time and energy for individual or collective action aimed at improving our society.
By the end of the last century, women united around common causes and formed organizations to fight for such issues as women's suffrage, temperance, abolition of child labour, and better working conditions and social justice for all.
Today, hundreds of women's groups continue this tradition of social struggle and involvement in areas such as family violence, sexual exploitation of children, employment equity and equality rights.
Our Government supports and encourages the work being done by women's groups.
During our previous term, Mr. Speaker, women and women's groups took an active part in developing government policy. Although the Department of the Secretary of State's Women's Program is the main source of financing for women's groups, the federal Government also helps these groups in other ways.
For instance, Mr. Speaker, women's groups have set up a number of projects thanks to the Child Care Special Initiatives Fund, created in December 1987 to promote innovation in daycare. In response to government initiatives to deal with family violence announced last June, women's groups have submittted projects for helping women who are victims of family violence, especially Native women, handicapped women and women who are immigrants or belong to visible minorities.

September 26, 1989
Government Orders
In Canada today, women and women's groups know that the concept of equality goes beyond the absence of discrimination.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today in support of this motion, but before I return the debate to the motion from whence it has diverted for the last 10 minutes, I would like first of all, through you, Mr. Speaker, to apologize most humbly to the hon. member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore for the uppity nature of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women for having the temerity to exercise its right to free speech when his committee was holding hearings in the city of Toronto.
May I further say that it is an edifying experience for the women in this House to be lectured to by the hon. member on the subject of how well off we are today. I hesitate to speak, of course, for my female colleagues on the other side of the House, but I can say for those of us over here that we just love having this gentleman telling us how lucky we are. I hope he might come some time to my constituency again and I can introduce him to large groups of women who perhaps may disagree with him. However, let us get back to the motion at hand.
I particularly support this motion in its reference to the declaration on the elimination of all discrimination against women, and I would like to note one of the articles of this. I quote:
Discrimination against women, denying or limiting as it does their equality of rights with men, is fundamentally unjust and constitutes an offence against human dignity.
And this is what we are talking about here today. We are not talking about how well off we are because we are not well off, not even those of us who have had the nerve to invade the sacred chambers normally inhabited by men. We are not well off, and women in this country are not well off. Working and fighting in the battle for gender equality is sometimes very depressing. I may say never more so than during the time I had to listen in the last 10 minutes.
The cuts in funding to hard-pressed women's groups are a travesty. One of those groups, I might mention, is the Canadian Congress of Learning Opportunities for Women, one of the most prestigious and respected groups that is doing a superb job of work for the advancement and for the equality of women in this country.
It is interesting about CCLOW. Do you know that CCLOW has written three times asking to meet with the Secretary of State. Does it have an appointment? Not yet! Has it had an answer to any of its letters? Not yet! But that is okay, we are well off and we do not need CCLOW to meet with the Secretary of State. As yet, no answer to three requests to meet. Yet the Secretary of State gives funding to REAL. I refuse to refer to it as "real". If that is "real" then the rest of us are extremely imaginary.
It is time for someone to get real around here and I say it is this government. This is the 20th century. You may have to be dragged kicking and screaming into it, but it is here. As a matter of fact it is almost over, so you had better hurry up.
The concept of family in this country has changed. The nuclear family with father working and bringing home the bacon and mother living in a rose-covered cottage and caring for the children is not the norm any more. Good or bad, it is not the norm.
The economic exigencies of modem life demand that women work outside the home. They have always worked inside the home, contrary to the belief of some people I have spoken to lately, but now they must work outside the home. The number of women who have the luxury of the choice to stay at home is getting smaller and smaller. Most people realize this, but some do not.
Women do not work for a lark and they do not work for a hobby, they work to survive. They work to support themselves, they work to support their children, they work to support aging relatives and so on and so on. Mainly they do this work for 35 per cent less money than men, and mainly they work in job ghettos.
But I will tell you a secret. Maybe we had better have water! Where are the pages? Just be ready with water Some women actually work in this country because they like to. They want to work, they enjoy it! And indeed these women manage to do a good job in the workplace. They manage, through some superhuman ability, to run their houses, to bring up children who do not turn into
September 26, 1989

young offenders, or drug addicts, or murderers, or even politicians. These women manage to keep all these balls in the air and they do it on less money and less time than anyone else has ever been asked to perform such herculean tasks with.
They do it without proper benefits, in the main. They certainly do it without adequate child care, and they do it in many, many cases without a real chance of promotion. They do it also with the reality of sexual harassment. It is not a pretty picture and, unfortunately, it is often a picture without much chance of advancement.
The declaration on the elimination of all kinds of discrimination against women refers to dignity. Let me tell you, it is an assault upon the dignity of Canadian women for the government to fund groups that do not believe in the principle of equality.
Hear, hear!

It is an assault on this dignity when groups who oppose pay equity, oppose child care and oppose the full inclusion of women at all stratas of society, are given credibility through government support.
There is no doubt that individual Canadians have a perfect right to believe that women should stay at home. Indeed, women who freely choose to work at home deserve our respect and also our support, but no one has the right to say that women must stay at home. No one has the right to deny women in the workforce the action necessitated by 2,000 years of patriarchal sexism, which will bring them to true equality.
There is an old Chinese principle that says women hold up half the sky. Actually it was Mao The Tung who said it and I think he was being a little conservative, probably for the one time in his life. Millions of women in this country carry the burden of home and workplace, provider and nurturer.
It has been 22 years since Canada signed the declaration on an end to all forms of discrimination against women. It has been five and a half years since the Charter of Rights and Freedoms came into force in Canada and sadly, unhappily, we are not much further ahead, in spite of the litany that I heard from my friend opposite.
Government Orders
Women have been patient but this patience is wearing very thin. Dignity means human, legal and civil rights. It means fair payment. It means fair opportunity. To a government that funds groups that deny these rights to women, I say, through you, Mr. Speaker, be warned by their works you shall know them. Cuts to groups that work for gender equity, combined with funding to groups who want to return us to the Dark Ages will be remembered.
I would like to close my comments a little early and quote a male poet if I may. If you think women won't remember that no action has been taken, I remind you of the words of John Donne "for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee".

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique B. Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I may say I listened with great interest to what my colleague, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Boyer), had to say. By recalling various projects that were also instrumental in promoting and improving the status of women in Canada, I feel he made a contribution towards achieving the objectives we have in mind, and I must say I appreciate that very much.
I listened earlier to what was being said by my colleague from the Liberal Party, and I find it hard to believe that today, in Canada, there are people who do not realize that the status of women in this country has made significant progress in the last ten years.
We need only look around us to realize that more and more, Canadian women are taking their rightful place, not the place of others but the place they deserve in various activity sectors.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to look at what is happening in education. Today, Laval University, which I happen to know best because it is practically next door . . .the statistics reveal that at Laval University in Quebec City, 52 per cent of the student population is female and I think this reflects what is happening across Canada. Mr. Speaker, this is indeed an improvement. My point is that if we want to achieve women's equality in employment and in all other areas, we first have to ensure that all women are entitled to a real education and to the same education as the population of Canada as a whole. Personally, I am proud of these figures, and I think that over the years we will see the results as our society evolves even more rapidly.

September 26, 1989
Government Orders
Mr. Speaker, Agnes MacPhail, the first woman to be elected to Parliament nearly sixty years ago, would probably be very proud to see that her pioneering efforts have bom fruit and that women are getting closer and closer to the common goal they have set for themselves, namely, equality on all fronts.
Mr. Speaker, if we look at the election held yesterday in Quebec, 121 candidates were fielded by the various political parties. By the end of the day, 22 women had been elected to the National Assembly. In one riding, people knew even before the results were announced yesterday that they would have a woman representing them in the National Assembly. In the riding of Kamou-raska-Temiscouata, three women were represented the various political parties: the Liberal Party, the Parti Quebecois and the Green Party. I don't think anyone protested the fact that all three candidates were women, three women who I am sure are trying to promote the status of all women and who do so despite their philosophical differences which, of course, we must respect.
A large number of Canadian women have reached the higher echelons in management and take part in the decisions that concern them as women. They constitute a group of first-rate spokespersons for all Canadian women.
Conversely, I believe that the women's movement's fundamental objectives of social, legal and economic equality are now shared by the vast majority of Canadian men and women.
This does not mean we can sit back and feel that women's equality is now a fact. On the contrary, we must intensify our efforts to pursue and attain the freedom we are seeking, as members of a society that respects the rights of each and everyone.
True to the spirit of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the Canadian Government tries to ensure that all Canadians participate equally in all aspects of life in this country. It recognizes the importance of promoting full participation by women in our country's political, social and economic life, and it has shown a strong commitment in the form of various initiatives.
The Government's main priorities with respect to the status of women are largely defined in a document entitled: Dimensions of Equality: A Federal Work Plan For Women. Its objective is to promote women's equality and remove barriers that limit their potential. The Women's Program, created almost 16 years ago, has drawn much of its inspiration from this work plan.
Since 1973, the Women's Program, which comes under the Department of the Secretary of State, has supported the initiatives of a large number of organizations dedicated to improving the status of women.
The Royal Commission of Inquiry On The Status of Women was right to recommend creating this kind of program.
Today, as a major federal program, it offers consulting services, information and financial assistance to groups that work for women, whether they are at home or on the labour market.
One of the goals of the Women's Program is to make governments, large institutions and the general public familiar with women's views on the burning issues of the day. And I wish people would not discriminate against the concerns of women generally. This makes the program an invaluable tool for all Canadian women.
During its first term, the present Government also placed special emphasis on women with special needs. And if you do not believe that handicapped women have special needs, you would do well to go back and see your constituents!
For example, the Secretary of State Women's Program gave financial assistance to the Disabled Women's Network to enable it to conduct a major national survey of the concerns of handicapped women. I think that is important; they are indeed very special needs and those people must be looked after.
In short, in 1987-88, the program financed nearly 750 national and regional projects which all contributed in one way or another to advancing the status of women in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, we have accomplished much in very little time. Of course, we firmly intend to continue in this way.
September 26, 1989

The record of our accomplishments on women's issues is most favorable, but I believe that women deserve most of the credit. We must also point out the sustained efforts of all concerned and hope that governments, institutions, unions and the private sector will continue to work together to make the necessary changes to our national life to promote justice and equal opportunity for all Canadians, men and women, individually and collectively.
Mr. Speaker, it is in this spirit that the Government undertakes to meet the formidable challenge of equality between men and women.
Mr. Speaker, fortunately, or maybe unfortunately, the member has concluded now, but my point of order was to ask you to rule on relevancy because not once did she address the motion.

Mr. Speaker, before I begin my speech in support of my colleague's motion I would like to point out that the members opposite have sent a rallying cry today for the feminist movement. As the feminist movement has always been fuelled by anger, you have given us more fuel for that struggle today in your comments.
I think the motion that my colleague has presented in the House also speaks to the kind of anger that the women of Canada have voiced against this government's actions in funding anti-equality groups. Not only on this side of the House but before the Health and Welfare Committee the Minister responsible for the Status of Women is quoted as saying that she was "damn mad" about that and that she was going to find out. We have not heard anything more, but I can assure you that feminist anger is not necessarily a politically partisan anger. It is an anger throughout this land for people who fund anti-equality.
When the Royal Commission on the Status of Women was brought forth 22 years ago it was for the promotion of equality and we will not be satisfied until that equality is attained, we will not be quiet, and we will not even be polite.
Hear, hear.

This is not a free speech issue. This is an issue on fighting for the kind of equality that we demand. We have a proud history in my party. The first woman member of Parliament, Agnes Macphail, was a member of my party. That long history of fighting for women's equality is something that we on this side, in this party, will be determined to continue, unlike some of the other people in this House.
Government Orders
We will not be satisfied with funding for band-aid solutions, the kind of solutions that the parliamentary secretary was alluding to in his talk. We are talking about funding for the real root causes against discrimination against women.
How will these groups do it with a 15 per cent reduction? They will have to go out and fund raise again. I am sure that is the concerted intention of the government, because the more energy groups put into fundraising the less they do in effecting real change in their communities.
I had the honour this year of writing a letter of support for a woman in my community who has spent her life working for the equality of women. Ms. Kay Armstrong has now just been selected to be one of the recipients of the Person's Award. This kind of lifetime work is what we, in my party, support.
The parliamentary secretary made his speech-I am careful now in my choice of language, Mr. Speaker, because I want to remain parliamentary but to say that I was offended by it is to understate somewhat.
This motion goes to the very heart of what this government talks about when we speak about deficit reduction and about cutting to the bare bones. We have to discriminate on what kind of money we spend. We have to target the use of funds wisely in order to achieve government objectives. So this is why it is not consistent to fund anti-equality groups if the government is sincere in its intention to promote the equality of women. This is why my colleague has put this motion forward. If you are sincere in wanting to cut the deficit and make your use of government funds more effective and if you want to promote the equality of women, the two things do not jive. You cannot have both. It is a shame that this government does not seem to have the real basis of understanding.
Prior to being elected I was active in a women's group in my community and I was privileged to be selected to talk on the funding issue to the standing committee which travelled across Canada. That message came through over and over again. When you are talking about a 15 per cent reduction for women's groups that are struggling for equality you are talking about reducing funds for women's centres that are working on sexual assault, you are talking about rural women who have very, very little opportunity for getting these kinds of resources in small communities. You are talking about women in major urban centres that have been on the vanguard of trying to see the whole infrastructure that discriminates against women.

September 26, 1989
Government Orders
When you are talking about that 15 per cent reduction you are talking about the real effects, the struggles we are trying to identify. It is child care issues, it is housing issues; all of these issues these women are trying to solve. The women's program is one of the most effective, efficient operations in trying to get the real structures of society changed. They get very good value for their money.
A number of my friends work in women's centres and they work for very little money. I am talking about an annual income of probably $22,000 or $23,000 a year, if they are lucky. They work many long hours for those salaries. So when you are talking about a 15 per cent reduction you are talking about cutting those salaries, cutting their efficiency and their ability to do their work.
This is why we find it so offensive that this government has decided to give a grant for the anti-equality group. It is just so inconsistent with all the government's intentions. I know that this government has a little problem with consistency, but this is one of the most blatant examples of it. The government is trying to talk out of one side of its mouth saying one thing and out of the other side saying another.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I just want to reiterate that the members opposite today have helped us enormously because they have fuelled that feminist anger. I know a number of journalists have now said that feminism is the new "f" word. Well, if that is the way they think of it, they can be assured that there are those women on this side of the House who are willing to say it over, and over again.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member for New
Westminster-Coquitlam has brought forward a motion which objects to the fact that the federal government has recognized the existence of an organization known as REAL and it has funded it, for one event, to the tune of $21,000 over against something like $11 million that was given to other women's groups and organizations. Now I do not know if that is a threat to the other organizations
but I do not understand why $21,000 is seen as such a threat, at least as indicated by this motion.
I listened to the remarks of the hon. member from New Westminster. She referred to the inequality that this organization proposes. And then I remembered seeing the masthead-you can understand I have not been active in that organization-of some of their literature and I see lawyers in the leadership and doctors and teachers and other professional people. I cannot imagine that the leadership of that organization considers itself to be in any way unequal to any other women's group and certainly not unequal to any men. They have made it and they have done very well. They have made it because they are good. I do not think they see themselves as being unequal to anyone, because they are professional people, whatever walk of life they are pursuing.
It is characteristic, however, of the New Democratic Party in its approach to life that it espouses causes of such things as tolerance, understanding and broadmindedness. NDP members really believe that if you happen to agree with them. They tend to be tolerant and broad-minded if you agree with them. But let anybody be different from them, let anybody cross swords with them, let anybody espouse a cause that argues with them and pretty soon we have names like Fascist and Klu Klux Klan coming up in the debate and somehow the tolerance and the understanding, all that goal seeking on the part of the New Democratic Party, somehow evaporates very quickly if somebody disagrees with them.
I happen to believe that there is some merit in this motion. I think perhaps groups that fight for the wrong causes, perhaps even in their definition, should not be funded. I recollect that when this organization put forward its conference there were demonstrations against it by other women's groups funded by the federal government. And I am saying to myself, if these women's groups are being funded by the federal government to fight for equality for women, which is a legitimate cause because we know that there are areas of inequality in the workplace and so forth, should they be using that funding to fight other women's groups who do not agree with them?
September 26, 1989
Don't patronize us.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
You see, I happen to put forward another point of view and so right away I am patronizing. Please, I thought we were all equal in this chamber.
So here we have women's groups who fight other women's groups but they do not want the other women's groups to get funds because they say that they are unequal. I tend to think that perhaps there is some merit in this motion and that the minister ought to pay some attention to it.
The other thing that bothers me about the remarks is that I thought they were somewhat inaccurate. I have read some of the literature of this organization and I recall very clearly that they support day care, perhaps not in the formula that the hon. member wants to see it. I remember reading that they-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
You can see the approach they take. This is equality of opinions here, you see. I recall that they believe in homemakers' pensions, perhaps not in the formula that some of the other women's groups suggest but they believe in it. Yet we were told in the chamber here that they do not support those causes. If we are going to debate these issues, we at least should be accurate.
I thought that the base definition of equality was that it suggests that we are equal even though we are not uniform, even though we are different we are equal. Surely in a world of diversity of ideas, in a country where there is a free flow of ideas, there ought to be room for diversity of opinion among women's groups. Surely that ought not to threaten the equality of any of those groups and certainly should not cause other women's groups to inveigh on the integrity and the viability of such groups that have a different point of view.

EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CRISIS IN CHINA-MANDATE OF UNITED NATIONS/EVACUATION PLANS FOR CANADIANS IN CHINA
['The motion to adjourn the House is now deemed to have been adopted. Accordingly, this House stands adjourned until tomorrow at 2 p.m., pursuant to Standing Order 24(1).']

Mr. Speaker, I note that you noticed me first this time.
On June 5, 1989, we passed a motion in this House unanimously condemning the government of China for the murder of hundreds of Chinese students in Tiananmen Square.
Two days later, on June 7, I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs what action he has taken to persuade the United Nations Security Council to intervene directly as the crisis, though internal, posed a potential and imminent threat to global peace and security.
On both occasions the Secretary of State assured this House that the situation was being treated very seriously by the government and, in fact, that relations between China and Canada would not be "business as usual", until the Chinese government put, and I quote the Secretary of State:
-a stop to the senseless killing and adopt a course of dialogue with the people of China.
These are Minister Clark's own words.
He went on to say that all events that were planned in the immediate future had been deferred or cancelled, that the signing of certain memorandums of understanding had been postponed, that nuclear co-operation consultations that were supposed to be ongoing had been suspended, and that visits were being deflected. In other words, everything was put on hold until such a time as the government of China would take some action to justify why in the light of recent events we should continue relations with that country.

September 26, 1989
Adjournment Debate
Well, as we all know now, this was not to be. Within two months of these assurances, the government decided to go ahead with a $1 million loan for the sale of Canadian telephone equipment. Within two months of these assurances the government decided to go ahead with an additional $130 million loan for a hydroelectric project in China. Within two months of these assurances the government decided to go ahead and send a federal civil servant to a conference run by the Chinese government in the month of November.
All this was after a reported private meeting that the Secretary of State had with the Chinese foreign minister during the July conference on Cambodia. We must also remember that while this private meeting was going on, the House was in recess and the Prime Minister and Mr. Clark were still spewing forth about the tough action that the government was taking against China.
We are now hearing from China's new consul general in Toronto that, and I quote his words: "Both countries' foreign ministries have met and that the Canadian government has expressed its willingness to restore normal relations between the two countries". This is a man who, in the same breath, justified the murder of those students in Tiananmen Square and the ongoing executions by the very fact that they are different concepts of human rights depending on different ideologies.
This kind of action from a country that prides itself on its reputation for leadership in human rights issues all over the world is abhorrent. When the loss of lives is ignored in the interest of a dollar, it is time to re-examine our priorities. It is in the interest of the dollar that this government has decided to turn a blind eye to the atrocities that still continue in China today.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs claims that it would be far more dangerous to stop all relations with China. What he means is that it would not do Canada any good financially to stop relations with China. Our trade with China and the virtually untapped market that is in China may forever be closed to us if we were to be firm and to insist that our continual relations would depend vastly on a change in the attitude of the Chinese Government.
This type of inconsistent and contradictory behaviour brings to mind the future of those Chinese who are still here in Canada. One begins to wonder what the definition of turmoil is to this government. The Minister of Immigration has assumed that no Chinese nationals will be sent back to China while there is still turmoil in their homeland. If the government is so willing to maintain its relationship with China under the present circumstances, how long before it decides either that things have returned to normal or that it cannot afford the wrath of the Chinese government with which it needs to do business so desperately?
It is ironic that the Secretary of State is on a five day visit to the United Nations Assembly, with human rights at the top of his agenda. I hope for his sake that he is not asked to respond to his government's handling of this particular situation.
After much lobbying Canada got its seat on the Security Council. To date we have been shy to use our position to address any crisis that has occurred since then. I am thinking of the China crisis, and the Syrian-Lebanese crisis.
On October 1 of this year we will be presiding over the council for a period of one month. I would question whether for this government all these accomplishments are really anything more than exercises in diplomatics and public relations.
Over the last few years the United Nations has developed into a body that has gained wide acceptance and admiration because it is able to wield great influence. Therefore it gets things done. I sincerely hope the question of China is still on the agenda and, if not, that this government will push to have it put on the agenda as the number of arrests and executions continue to mount. I know that the parliamentary secretary has to reply on behalf of the minister. My criticism is not addressed to the parliamentary secretary, but at the way his government handled this situation. I know of his interest in human rights around the world. He knows that human rights violations have no borders. I know if he were the Secretary of State for External Affairs he would have handled it differently.

speakeroldname: Mr. Patrick Boyer (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park is a thoughtful and experienced parliamentarian. Although this is a sensitive and, in many ways, a difficult issue I am glad that he has raised it.

At the conclusion of the debate in this House, the Secretary of State for External Affairs put forward a resolution which was adopted by all parties. It gave expression to three guiding principles that would try to frame Canadian policy in relation to China, following the tragedy of June.
The three basic principles that the Secretary of State outlined were these. First, to preserve existing links to the extent possible; second, to focus on people-to-peo-ple exchanges; and, third, there would be no support from Canada for the military and propaganda apparatus of China.
Now, it is very clear that in this matter we are walking a fine line. It is not an easy matter or always a black and white, simplistic matter to say we are expressing our condemnation of the Chinese regime and those actions. At the same time, we want to see China not revert into isolation where, unfortunately, it was for a quarter of a century, and that the links that have patiently been developed between our country and China not all be jeopardized at the same time. So it is clearly a difficult tight rope or fine line that any government of whatever persuasion would be walking. That, I think, was reflected in the unanimous resolution passed here.
I can say that the Secretary of State has publicly expressed the view that the two subsequent actions to which the hon. member has referred are consistent with the criteria that he has set out.
The further and final point I want to make is that the member referred to an official of the Chinese Government who had referred to a return to normalcy in Canadian-Chinese relations. Those were the Chinese official's words. That was his interpretation. That was in his interest to state, but that does not reflect the position of the Government of Canada. It does not reflect the position of where the government is going on this.
Chinese in this country, the students particularly, the guarantees that were given by the government stand. There will be no mass returning of people or of individuals who participated here. What was committed by the government stands as government policy.
Adjournment Debate
REPORT-COMPENSATION FOR VICTIMS/REQUEST FOR EARLY ANNOUNCEMENT

rise today with regard to a question posed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare on April 20, 1989.
On that particular occasion I requested of the minister responsible for health and welfare that a commitment be made and a subsequent decision thereafter be made in terms of providing compensation to those individuals who were affected with the thalidomide drug some time ago. On that occasion, the minister indicated to the House and to members present that no decision would be forthcoming until a comprehensive review could be undertaken.
I rise tonight to underline the seriousness of the request, the importance of compensation to those courageous young men and women who have been affected with this particular disability.
Some time ago the report of the thalidomide task force indicated the following: "The responsibility of the federal government to provide compensation for the victims of thalidomide was admitted in a statement made to a special committee of the House of Commons on January 29, 1963; by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Hon. J. Waldo Monteith. The minister at that time said: It is our job to ensure that these victims are cared for in the best possible manner. . .and that their needs are met to the fullest possible extent we can devise".
That was a statement which was made by a previous minister of the Crown. The Government of Canada, and particularly the Department of Health and Welfare, have been seized with this particular issue for so many years, in fact, 26 years. Recently, a task force report which was submitted to the minister in February outlined veiy clearly why they believe, as victims, and the organizers as well, that the Government of Canada ought to share in some of the responsibility for this particular, what I deem, disaster.
Unfortunately, this government, as well as previous governments, have not moved very quickly. Yes, it can be said of the present administration that it only received the report several months ago and is not in a position to make that decision. We should reverse the situation for a moment. We should ask ourselves: "What are these victims doing? What sort of lifestyle are they enjoying in 1989? What are the demands made of them in every day living, from housing, to medicare, to education and

Adjournment Debate
training?" Their marketability in terms of the job market must also receive careful consideration. I believe more so it requires action by the Government of Canada. These are men and women who, because of no fault of their own, have had to put up for some many years with the effects of this particular drug.
I am perfectly well aware of the arguments which have been made by legal counsel for the Government of Canada that to admit liability in some way would be setting a precedent. I do not argue on the basis of legal precedent. I argue on the basis of a moral responsibility that the Government of Canada must have towards its citizens regardless of where they live and indeed the circumstances in which they do live.
The International Commission of Health Professionals supports the Canadian thalidomide victims' claim and has done so. In fact, a statement of claim has been submitted to the Subcommittee of the United Nations Commission on Human Rights for its determination.
So this issue has now transcended, if you will, Canadian boundaries and is in the hands of the United Nations for a decision as to what it believes to be appropriate. I would like to ask through you, Mr. Speaker, to the parliamentary secretary, as to whether or not an affirmative decision can be made forthwith in order to provide the necessary compensation to alleviate some of the harm and some of the difficulties that these individuals have been confronted with for so many years. Second, is the minister prepared to stop putting preconditions in terms of compensation, and would he meet again, as he has in the past, with the organizers and the thalidomide victims to discuss in detail as to how compensation is provided and how it ought to be administered over an extended period of time?
In conclusion, I wish to say that this particular issue has received the support of many of my colleagues on this side of the House. I name two in support of what I am saying here today. My colleague from London East, as well as my colleague from Dartmouth, are both very supportive, as is our entire caucus, to the idea of providing the necessary compensation. I suggest, however, to the parliamentary secretary responding on behalf of the minister that that response is long overdue. I would hope that he will provide us with some positive news as to when the compensation will be forthcoming.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many of us in the House remember the shock and sadness that accompanied the birth of the thalidomide babies around the world in the early 1960s. This unhappy event represented a profound challenge to the understanding and endurance of the medical and scientific communities and ultimately to the spirit and well-being of the thalidomide victims themselves.
At that time the federal government arranged with the provinces a cost-shared plan of assistance and support to thalidomide victims and their families. The program addressed not only the medical needs of the children but also the economic, psychological and social impact of the tragedy on those affected and the enhancement of rehabilitation services. The federal government was able to stimulate these co-operative efforts through four programs: national health grants, national welfare grants, the medical rehabilitation crippled children's program and the hospital insurance program.
The government pursued the recommendations of an expert committee established in 1962 to examine the habitation of congenital anomalies with thalidomide and funded professional training for clinical rehabilitation workers, the establishment of regional prosthetic research and training centres and schools of prosthetics.
As the issue of financial compensation from the drug manufacturers developed, the government offered families of thalidomide victims whatever assistance they might require in presenting their cases to the company. A number of families took advantage of this offer and received settlement through this route.
In 1988, the War Amputations of Canada gathered together for the first time a number of Canadian thalidomide victims and out of this meeting grew the Thalidomide Victims Association of Canada and the Thalidomide Task Force. The task force prepared an extensive report of the Thalidomide tragedy and submitted its work to the Department of National Health and Welfare on February 14, 1989.
The government's review of the positions and perspectives presented by the task force began immediately. Central to the current issue is the task force's request for financial compensation on behalf of all surviving thalidomide victims in Canada.
On March 30, the Hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare met with representatives of the task force and the Thalidomide Victims Association in Toronto. The meeting provided all participants with an opportunity to exchange ideas and views. Several members of the task force and the association described the needs and
September 26, 1989

aspirations of thalidomide victims in eloquent terms. The minister explained the process by which he and his officials are attempting to address their concerns and their requests, and those of other groups of Canadians who have represented their cases to the government.
This first meeting was an occasion to learn but the process is by no means complete. There has been substantial correspondence between the minister and the task force aimed at keeping open the lines of communication. We are confident this process can lead toward a shared appreciation of a basis on which extraordinary assistance can be extended.
Adjournment Debate
It would not be true to the spirit of this process to prematurely speculate on the outcome, but thalidomide victims and others with requests now before the government need to be assured that their needs and concerns are being heard and considered with the utmost importance.
